speechtext:

to a vote by the Parliament of Canada to, the provinces for health purposes. Take one instance, the steamship Glenclova, which was valued in the exhibit handed to the commission at $525,000. The net earnings after deducting depreciation for the year ending December 31, 1921, exceeded five times the amount required for interest on this issue.

Now, I have dealt briefly with causes; let me refer for a moment to the effects of the concentration of wealth. According to the Canada Year Book for 1922-23, .14 per cent of those who paid income tax had 25.77 per cent of the total income; .42 per cent of the taxpayers,-that is, less than one-half of one per cent-had 37.73 per cent of the income, while 7.7 per cent of the taxpayers had 74.80 per cent of the income. I want to point out that this is only the percentage of the amount of income of those whose incomes were taxable. After all, it is only a small proportion of the population who have incomes that are taxable under the Income Tax Act; so that when we figure it out on the proportion of the income, of the whole population we find that a very much greater percentage of wealth is in the hands of a few than these figures would indicate. In reference to the income tax figures of the United States, I find that in 1918, 14 per cent of the income taxpayers had 40 per cent of the total income. In this connection I would also like to quote a former chancellor of the exchequer of Great Britain, Mr. Snowden, who, speaking in the British House of Commons on March 20, 1923, said:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question that the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) has brought before the House this afternoon is a technical one, a complicated and an interesting one. He has cited a number of cases where companies have made large earnings because of what he calls the watering of stock, and the paying of dividends on. stock which was of no value. The resolution seems very innocent as it stands on the order paper, but it has one or two features which present difficulties. Before we could accept the resolution that my hon. friend has so ably put forward, we would first have to have some definition of "watered stock". Watered stock may be of different varieties. It might be stock such as my hon. friend has described, for which the holder gives no particular value. Stock may also be described as watered that is issued for the purchase of goodwill, or anything of that kind. A company taking over the assets of another company may pay in stock for such things as that. Such an asset may have no tangible value, but nevertheless it is of some value.
For many years, the several provinces of the Dominion have grappled with this question. I was unable to hear my hon. friend very distinctly, but I think he did refer to the different provinces that had grappled with this question to some extent. Some of the provinces have issued what are called blue sky 'laws to protect the public from the sale of stock by companies, and I think the Supreme Court of Canada has recently brought down a judgment declaring that the legislation passed in the province of Saskatchewan in that respect was ultra vires of the provincial legislature. I might also say to my hon. friend that the officials of the department under whose control and administration the Companies Act comes have given a very
great deal of study to this question for many years, and I have several reports before me in regard to it; I have one very lengthy one before me now. The question my hon. friend has raised is not without its difficulties. A company is organized, and an application is made for its incorporation, either to the provincial legislature or to the Dominion. The company sets forth its object, and obtains its charter. All that is pretty well safeguarded, in -so far as we are able to do so. The issuing of stock is practically a matter of civil contract between the company and the purchaser of the stock. My hon. friend has referred to cases where companies have made large a.nd unreasonable profits because of stock watering, and that as a result of watering their products were sold at a higher price to the public in order that they could pay dividends on the watered stock. Nevertheless, people are not forced to buy these products.

Under the Dominion charter, as I remember it, we have regulations by which the company that is issuing stock fraudulently or by misrepresentation may be called to account by the department. As regards the issuing of stock in the ordinary way, and charging a higher price for it, I am not in a position to say that some scheme might not be worked out and legislation enacted that would bring about an improvement. I can assure my hon. friend, and I think I can speak not only for the government but for every individual member of parliament, that if anything can be done to better conditions or to pass legislation to bring about an improvement along the line of meeting my hon. friend's complaint, it will be not only a pleasure for me but a duty, and the duty of this parliament, to do it. My hon. friend has brought the matter to the attention of the House and of those particularly interested in this matter, and when they read his remarks in Hansard, they will be able to gather what he has in his mind. exactly what I said and what I meant. The government is prepared and willing to bring down any amendment that will remedy the difficulty, and will be very glad of suggestions from the hon. member. T think when sug-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
We have surely a rather anomalous
situation. The members of the government readily admit that we have in Canada such a thing as watered stock, although we may differ a little in our definition of it. They also admit that the watering of stock, that is, the issuance of stock for which no value is given to the public, is an evil, and yet the government, notwithstanding the fact that this matter has been repeatedly brought to their attention, appear to be incapable of devising any means of doing away with this evil. Those of us who are neither legal gentlemen nor financiers sometimes wonder why it is, when it comes to the matter of the great vested interests that the government find themselves in the position of being impotent to take any action which will safeguard the interests of the public. If it is the case of some milkman diluting his milk with water, action can be taken very speedily to stop the practice, without any question as to whether or not the water is pure or impure, alkali water or spring water. We urge that the essence of our representations is that the public is being defrauded. The common people and this government are agreed that the public has been defrauded by the process known as the watering of stock. And yet apparently year after year when the subject has been introduced the matter has been put off, as the government would seek to put it off to-day. Many cases of special privilege come before this House. Whenever we introduce any other than one or two well recognized types, we are said to be dealing with an academic question. I submit that the public is very much concerned about a matter of this kind. I quote here a paragraph which I noticed in a recent editorial of the Quebec Daily Telegraph in which we have noted the close connection between watered stock and the tariff. The editorial reads:
We trust that all those who are crying blue ruin for Canada, on account of tariff reductions or lack of action to raise them, will not fail to let the public know whether or not Canada is going to continue *o protect hundreds of millions of dollars of watered stock which periodically floods a number of our industrial concerns, when their profits become so large that they are afraid of public criticism.
On the other hand, if the Ottawa government is being asked to protect merged industries that contain millions of dollars worth of watered stock for the benefit of a few promoters this information should nJso accompany the blue rum speeches on the tariff question.

Watered Stock
We also think that the federal government shol"J at once institute an investigation into the watered stock capitalization of many merged industries, which are crying for further protection.
I would commend that paragraph to the serious consideration of the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp).
We have before us at the present time the far-reaching results of the failure of the Home Bank. I take it that one of the resons for this failure was that the bank advanced money to concerns which were not sound, which were putting before the country propositions Which involved watered stock. Now the country is being asked to reimburse the Home Bank depositors and yet we are doing nothing to preclude frauds of this kind being perpetuated in the future.
We are to-day facing the very serious consideration of some action in connection with the industrial dispute in the Nova Scotia coal fields. It has been repeatedly called to the attention of this government that the British Empire Steel Corporation has been trying to insist upon dividends oh what we generally know as watered stock. I had an opportunity a year ago of calling the attention of the government to the way in which the capitalization of that corporation had been built upon. I will not repeat here what I said at that time, but it is known that the company, in seeking incorporation, had to admit that it w'ould not require a very great deal to finance the company that it was proposed to create. A little later on, the promoters were able to inflate the capital to a very great extent. I have a memorandum with [DOT] regard to the organization of that company:
The Dominion Iron and Steel Company Limited was incorporated in 1899, H. M. Whitney of Boston being the chief promoter. He had previously organized the Dominion Coal Company. Whitney wrote to Premier Murray asking for concessions in the royalty on coal used in the new steel plant. In that letter he said:
*' The estimate of an iron plant in Cape Breton on a large scale would require the investment of a large sum of money, not less than $3,000,000 to $6,000,000."
This letter is published in the Industrial Advocate of Halifax for April, 1899.
The Engineering and Mining Journal of New York- issue of October 28-records the listing of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company on the Boston stock exchange. The company is stated to have $15,000,003 stock and $8,000,000 in bonds (of which latter $2,000,000 were still in the company's treasury). I
I do not know whether the government can justify anything of that kind. I do not know whether the country is compelled forever to pay dividends on stock of that character, but I know we must face the result of this situation in the low wages and dissatisfaction which prevail at the present time in Nova Scotia.
75i
Let me mention still another instance which recently came before the attention of the public. The L. R. Steel Company were able, through their manipulation, to victimize a large number of poor people throughout this country. This was done very largely through the practice to which reference has already been made, that of maintaining subsidiary holding companies. I think now of families in my constituency who could ill afford any loss of this character, who were approached by plausible agents of the L. R. Steel Company and were told that this was in the nature of a co-operative company. They believed in the principle of co-operation, and they were deceived as to the real standing of the company. An altogether different proposition was put up to them from that which would have been warranted by the facts of the case. We all know the results. I would like to refer to still another organization which has recently been before the public, especially in my city.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I am sure we can
depend on the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) to set us right in regard to matters of that kind. I would refer to another company and ask the Secretary of State to take particular notice of this. It is a company whose conduct has recently been forced upon our attention in the west, the Hearst Music Publishing Company. I am informed that this company had a Manitoba charter but it had been refused a license under the Sales
rMr. Meighen.]
of Shares Act. Then under pressure a license was granted. After a further examination, however, the license was withdrawn. The company then obtained a Dominion charter, thus being able to snap its fingers at the provincial government and at the public generally. Under these circumstances we have a perfect right to come to the Dominion government and ask that the interests of the public be protected.
I should like to read a paragraph or so from a statement which has been furnished me by a friend of mine who has been devoting some little attention to this matter. He suggests:
Watered stock is always a potential charge upon the workers, but where competition really exists its influence or effect upon labour conditions is inconsequential. When, however, a company operates uncitr the direction of a combine-
Such as that referred to a little while ago, the Canada Cement concern.
-or enjoys some special privilege, permitting it to charge unwarranted prices foi its commodities or services, then watered stock may readily become a serious evil. Canada happens to be a country where the financial system lends itself readily to the nationwide control of enterprises, either by means of combines, fixing market spheres or fixing prices. That fact gives to watered stock in Canada an importance which it does not always hold in other countries where the financial systems are less favourable to the establishment of centralized control of whole industries.
The writer then gives one method by which the public has often been victimized.
Another game which has been too often practised may be described. Two or three men owning similar enterprises may be bitten with the passion for easy money. They organize a company to amalgamate their enterprises. The new company makes a loud noise about the economies effected by the consolidation, and reports huge profits. Then the two or three men, having issued to themselves bonds representing something more than the value of the combined enterprises, send out salesmen to dispose of common stock in their company representing something more or less than its bond issue. Usually the stock is sold at par, if the declared profits said to have resulted from the amalgamation are high enough. The stock is bought by small investors who know nothing about the actual workings of the company, and seldom ask for information.
In a year or so the men who formed the company, having utilized the money derived from the sale of common stock in ways which may indirectly benefit them while adding nothing to the resources or capacities of the company, discover that that company is beset with difficulties. The common stock holders are informed that dt can only be saved by additional stock subscriptions, and being frightened usually do not respond. Presently the company declares itself bankrupt, and the original owners who hold the bonds take over the properties and the investors in common stock are left with finely engraved but perfectly valueless certificates. This game in various forms has been played by highly respectable financiers and lawyers, and fairly competent lawyers have been victims of it.

Watered Stock
I want to present to the House a few more paragraphs taken from a memorandum furnished by another friend of mine-a business man. It may seem rather strange that business men sometimes are willing to assist or to speak through Labour members in this House. This I sometimes think may perhaps be attributed to the fact that, as one of the old Socialist leaders once suggested, the workers having nothing to lose but their chains, are able to speak freely in these financial matters. Certainly, they are free to say what I know a great many business men across the country would gladly say. The excerpt to which I refer is as follows:
Perhaps it is not too much to say that the greatest controllable evil in connection with the " high cost of living " is the tendency which Canadian financiers have shown in the last few years, and in increasing numbers, to follow the high finance methods of American promoters. These methods vary so greatly that it is impossible to give more than an outline of them without writing a series of books, but the following are fair examples:-
A family is operating a manufacturing plant in a small town; they give individual attention to the business; they know all their workmen personally and they work in harmony with them, paying fair wages and making moderate but steady profits; the business grows, the line of goods becomes known and the trade mark established. The business begins to outgrow the old methods; new workmen are brought in for special new machines; the owners die; their sons are not content to run the business in the old way. The promoter appears on the scene, he has nothing but a good suit of clothes, a fine line of talk and a knowledge of American promoting methods. The promoter sizes up the business; perhaps the value at a conservative estimate is half a million dollars including buildings, real estate, machinery and stock on hand; but the hard work of the founders, their knowledge of the business, their lack of extra overhead put on iby so-called efficiency experts, and the small salaries that they are content to draw from their own business, and other factors, make the business pay on an average through a period of exception-ally good years, say one hundred thousand dollars a year. Does the promoter buy the business for five hundred thousand dollars (its actual value without the men that built it and the surroundings under which it was built) ? He does not. He searches for and finds a business that will go well in a prospectus with this business. He options this second business which is, 'for some reason we need not specify, not paying, at say one hundred thousand dollars payable partly in cash and partly in the stock of a new company. He options the first business, producing as you remember one hundred thousand dollars a year when trade is good. He gives the owners five hundred thousand dollars of preferred stock and five hundred thousand dollars of common stock; he puts them and himself on the board of directors and arranges salaries for them at least double the rate they have been drawing. He sells bonds to the public for five hundred thousand dollars. He can show earnings which provide three times the interest on the bonds. The second business takes perhaps fifty thousand dollars of the cash, the promotion takes another hundred thousand dollars to swing and the promoter, if he is fairly modest takes only another hundred thousand dollars in cash and five hundred thousand dollars of common stock. Part of his common stock he gives away with the bonds and some of it he gives to the owners of
the small business which has been taken in to show some reason for the water and make believe that it will increase the earning power of the first business or absorb some of its product.
Now let us see where we are. We had one business worth half a million dollars and earning on an average in good years, and when it had the benefit of the founder's experience and his undivided time and attention, one hundred thousand dollars a year. We had another business which was breaking even and which was worth, perhaps, fifty thousand dollars. That is, we had what, stripped of the special circumstances that made them pay, two businesses that were worth $550,000 of anybody's money and that only had to earn $33,000 to give their owners a reasonable return on their investment, or at any rate, would not normally be called on to part with more than $33,000 per annum to satisfy capital. What have we now? Bonds, $500,000; preferred stock, $500,000; common stock, $1,000,000; total $2,000,000. The public is now called upon to pay interest on two million dollars, fourteen hundred and fifty thousand of which is new capital created out of paper and the promoter's ideas. The public is now called upon to pay salaries sufficiently dignified to fit the officers of a two million dollar corporation and at least twice as much as the same individuals drew when the businesses were entirely their own. The public is now called upon to pay for efficiency experts, accountants instead of bookkeepers and all sorts of people who were not needed in the old business, which nine times out of ten, produced as much and as good material as cheaply without their aid.
One of two things happens, either the price of the product is increased and the wages of the lower employees decreased until the interest on the securities is paid, or the concern goes to the wall when the old management is withdrawn and the cost of production increased beyond what the product will bear. If the concern goes to the wall the men in the plant lose their jobs and the small investor who has absorbed the common and preferred stock is wiped out. The bond holders take over the property reorganize the company, rewater the stock and the same thing happens again. If the promoter has had luck the company goes on, pays its dividends and perhaps in time is ripe to be taken into a yet larger promotion and help to put more watered stock on the market. In either case the public is stuck. The promoter is all right; he has his cash and the proceeds of his common stock. The former owner may be all right. He may have sold his stock, and anyway he has the bonds and his property back. But the public is stuck whether the company is a success or a failure.
Every time one of these companies is a success the cost of living is raised to make it a success. Every time one of these companies is a failure the public is stuck. It is always the public who pay.
And this gentleman, who, as I say, is a business man, makes the following suggestion, which I give for what it is worth:
The only thing that can be done is to provide machinery for scrutinizing and licensing new issues of stock and bonds for public sale. The Secretary cf State department are quite competent to deal with this matter if they have the necessary legislation back of them. Governments naturally shirk the responsibility for stock issues but they must assume it or we will go from bad to worse. A few years ago-
And I think this calls attention to a tendency which we cannot disregard.
A few years ago preferred stocks were generally regarded as safe investments but the collapse of the Riordon and other companies has weakened the public
Watered Stock

confidence in preferred stock and the promoter now generally puts the bonds of his company before the public in the first stages of unloading. Bonds were sold during the war in such varied forms that a great many people are now interested in them who never heard of them before 1916 and to the ordinary small investor anything with coupons on it looks aa good as a government bond, consequently the money which once went to mortgages now goes into all sorts of bonds sold by promoters and it is difficult to get the necessary money for building and farm loans. This has forced up rents and increased the cost of living and it is likely that some of these bond issues will fall down and leave the promoter with the need of inventing another form of security to tempt the ever-gullible public. All this cannot be stopped but it can at least be diminished by periodical warnings to the public and by regulation.
Now, the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) has asked for specific suggestions. I would venture to say that if his own department is not prepared to carry out any such scrutiny as that suggested in this memorandum, probably the purpose in view would be accomplished equally well if the government would introduce an amendment providing that every company with a Dominion charter should come under the Sales of Shares Acts of the various provinces. That may not be going very far, but at least it is something concrete. In a number of our provinces to-day we have agencies, more or less successfully protecting the public with respect to companies that have provincial charters, but it seems that there is no way by which these provincial agencies can do anything to protect the public against a company with a Dominion charter. This suggested measure would require no additional machinery.
Before I take my seat I should like to call the attention of the Secretary of State to what seems to be a very admirable report on blue sky legislation made by Mr. A. H. O'Brien, and issued by order of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario. I note here that:
In 1895, Great Britain appointed a committee of the board of trade to look into the question. That committee made an exhaustive study of the entire problem through a period of years. In 1900 legislation was passed placing moderate restrictions on the issue of fictitious stock. This legislation not accomplishing its purpose, committees of both Houses of Parliament again considered the problem. In 1906 the present legislation was enacted, and it is now incorporated in the Companies Consolidation Act of 1908.
I notice that as far back as 1884 Germany passed laws limiting the sale of fraudulent securities, and France, in 1893, passed similar legislation. I notice also that the Ontario Companies Act is copied largely from the Companies Act of Great Britain, but does not include all of its provisions. Mr. O'Brien states:
When, under the British act, a prospectus is issued it must furnish very full information, not only of I Mr. Woodsworth.]
earnings and assets of all companies formed, but of all promoting, underwriting, selling and managing profits made from corporate promotions, including allotments of stock and ownership of stock. . . The prospectus, when filed, is open to the public, and requires full disclosure of all profits made directly or indirectly from the formation of corporations and officers must reveal fully all money made as a result of their connection with the corporation.
If that is possible in Great Britain, is it not possible in Canada? As to the effect of blue sky legislation in the state of Kansas, the commissioner states that:
The law has kept out of the state an immense amount of worthless securities. It has put some of the persistent violators in jail and has made refugees in other states of others. The law has not eliminated the sale of worthless stock, but has reduced it to a minimum.
The objection that it is dangerous for the state to intervene is, I think, met by the following statement:
Those persons that make such objections fail to realize that the corporation whose securities are being controlled has been created, and the issue of it3 securities authorized and sanctioned, by the state.
In 1921 a special commission appointed by the governor of Massachusetts to investigate the sale of corporate securities reported as follows:
Since the state authorizes the issuance of fictitious or watered stock, it must follow that it is the duty of the state to prevent the sale of such securities until the state itself determines that they are not fraudulent. The state creates the securities, and places them in the hands of the fraudulent promoter, who in turn distributes them to the public. Any additional legislation to check the sale of fraudulent securities is nothing more or less than an effort by the state to limit the use by fraudulent promoters of the false tokens which the state itself creates.
Now, it is not my purpose to read in detail any further extracts from this report, although it contains many passages of very-great importance.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Does the report that the hon. gentleman is reading from deal at all with the issue of watered stock, or merely with its sale after it is issued?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It deals with the sale of watered stock. But I am suggesting that this House might, as a preliminary step, pass legislation by which any company owning a Dominion charter would 'be able to sell its stock only under the laws which prevail in the various provinces. That is my point. Personally I should like to go much further than that, and it seems to me that the government must in the long run go much further. As the House knows, we have the insurance companies brought under cast-iron regulations, and whereas a few years ago there was a good deal of fraud connected with the various

Watered Stock
weaker companies, and especially with their promotion, to-day we have our superintendent of insurance whose duty it is to safeguard the public interest. Last year we made provision for an inspector of banks. The House will remember that two years ago such a measure was voted down on the ground that it was not possible for the state to interfere with the banks; but after the failure of the Home Bank the government came around to the position that it was essential that the public should be protected; and an inspector was appointed. Now, I suggest that, as we have a superintendent of insurance companies and an inspector of banks, it is not any very great innovation to advocate that it is the duty of the state to protect the public generally in this matter of stock manipulation, which, after all, is a much more complicated question than either of the other two to which I have referred.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all let me extend my deep sympathy to the government. The usual policy of evasion is to be continued on this as on most other matters. When I came down here I was practically given to understand that we should not have come as farmers or as representatives of any other political body than the Liberals, because they were going to give us everything we were advocating. Amongst the things we were advocating was the abolition of watered stock. Another thing was the abolition of protection -1a protective tariff. The government's attitude certainly must make its supporters in -the province of Quebec weep. I am sure they will mourn to-morrow when they read of the attitude of hon. members opposite with respect to the resolution -of the hon. -member for Mackenzie (Mr. -Campbell). I have in my hand an article printed by a paper about which I do not know very much-^proba-bly my hon. friends opposite do

the Quebec Telegraph. Does it represent them or support them at any time? The Quebec Telegraph has this to say:
Liberals are not against a tariff-
I heard the contrary during the elections. -but they are against a tariff which protects overwatered stocks of companies when they stop paying dividends because they have been cleaned out by the insiders. Such protection only benefits a handful of the controlling interests.
I wonder what the Quebec Telegraph will write about it to-morrow? I wonder what the labourers in -the cities of Montreal and in Quebec and Nova Scotia and the west will say? The average annual wage paid in all industries in 1917 was the pitiful sum of $757.
There is no doubt in the world that one of the chief causes for that low wage was the necessity of paying dividends on watered stock. In 1918 the average wage was $866, and in 1919 it was $940, war conditions compelling an increase. We find that of all salaries and wages to employees in all industries in 1919, the average per worker or salaried man was $1,010.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman go a little further? I have answered his question; now I want to put another to him. Will he say there is no such thing in industry in Canada as watered stock?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext: I am not speaking on that general subject. But I submit that before a company is said to be paying low wages on account of having watered stock, those who make the assertion should be prepared to prove it by the submission of evidence that would be accepted in a court of law.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will have to take issue with his own colleague and, I presume, political superior, the Minister of Labour. At any rate the fact of the matter is that industry in this country, despite the position taken by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell), is exacting unfair profits as a result of watered stock.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) was very anxious for definitions. I really had not gone to the bother of finding out the actual definition of watered stock; the thing appeared to be perfect^ clear to me. The popular idea of watered stock is that suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), and there should be very little trouble about that. But if we turn to another authority we find that Professor Irving Fisher, of Yale University, has discussed watered stock after this manner. In the discussion of certain methods under which the book value of capital, surplus and divided profits may exaggerate the true condition of the company, he goes on to point out another way in which that may be done, namely, through the issue of stock below par, or for services, patents, and so forth, at unduly high prices. He goes on to say:

To illustrate this way oi overvaluing capital, or " stock-watering," suppose a company to be capitalized at $200,000, and that this company issues at the beginning 1,000 certificates of the par value of $100,000, but sells them for only $60 per share actually paid into the treasury. Here is $60,000 paid-in capital, lepresented by $100,000 face value of stock certificates, leaving a margin of $40,000 " water." Suppose, further, that another block of $100,000 of the stock is given to an inventor for his patent, the real value of which is only $10,000. Finally, suppose that bonds are issued to the extent of $300,000, and are floated at par. Then the company has received in actual cash only $360,000. Of this sum only $60,000 has been received from the stockholders. The patent, which has also been contributed m return for $100,000 of stock, and which is worth only one-tenth of that sum, makes	the total	balance due the	stockholders$70,000. But, the company is capitalized at $200,000. Consequently	it will be	necessary for the	bookkeeperto exaggerate	the assets	to the extent of	$130,000. He
may do this as follows:
Assets	Liabilities
Plant (cost	$360,000)..	$400,000 Bonds	 $300,000
Patent (worth $10,000).	100,00 Capital.... 200,000
$500,000	$500,000
Here $90,000 of the exaggeration is put under patent and the remainder in an overvaluation of the plant. Many other methods of stock-watering are possible. A common one is to allow the plant to run down.
That is sometimes called mismanagement.
It is sometimes said that stock-watering is not wrong, as long as all the terms and conditions are known. This is much like saying that lying is not wrong, provided everybody knows that it is lying; lor a false balance sheet is oniy one form of a false statement, and, ordinarily, a false statement is made with the intent to deceive. The object may be, for instance, to mislead intending bondholders by making them believe that there is a larger security for their loans than actually exists. We see here one reason why honest men often undervalue their assets-
And so on. That, Mr. Speaker, is the learned opinion of Professor Irving Fisher in his book The Nature of Capital and Income, given at pages 79 and 80. I would suggest that that is one form of watered stock which has perhaps not come to the attention of the Secretary of State; but the undoubted fact i3 that in Canada, as in other countries, you have the vast body of the public called upon to pay dividends on watered stock for which no value has been given.
If you will turn to the table from which my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) has read, I would like now to sum it up. He mentioned several companies including the Amalgamated Asbestos Corporation, Ames-Holden-McGready, Limited, and the Canada Cement Company. I will take the Whole list and summarize it. Ninety-four companies came into various amalgamations, and were thereby reduced to 17 combines or mergers. The 94 companies had a total capitalization prior to amalgamation of $63,788,500. Upon that capital, I presume, they were paying

Watered Stock
dividends to the stockholders; but after amalgamation we find that these 17 corporations have a total capital of $206,650,000. The increase in the capital value of the above companies, authorized under tihe Companies Act is $142,861,500, or 324 per cent, and on that the company now expects to pay dividends. This situation unhappily is not confined to this country. Yet I will say that a certain condition in this country. tends to make the watering of stock a more common practice than in others. This condition is undoubtedly the special privilege of tariff protection which is extended to companies or corporations of the kind cited in these mergers. For example, where a tariff duty is raised so high that it prevents any reasonable competition in the home market, and gives to a corporation in the country complete or almost complete monopoly, and so control of the home market, undoubtedly that company is in a position not only to pay lower wages to the people it employs, but also to exact higher profits from the people who buy its goods. I would, therefore suggest to the minister, who is anxious for suggestions, and in the hope that his officials will do more than his government, that one of the means by which he could get over the British North America Act in regard to the British Empire Steel Corporation-and he was anxious that my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) would help him out in that regard-is to cut off all bounties on steel until the water is squeezed out of that stock. That would be one method.

speechtext:
What about
cement?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Exactly. I would suggest that with regard to other corporations or combines that have watered stock on which they may be exacting profits from the people, the protective tariff be removed entirely.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext: And cut out the special railway rates that some of these companies enjoy.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I have in my hand a further list of suggestions which possibly the Secretary of State has not seen. They were made by Professor Albion Small, a leading American sociologist, and appeared in the January issue of the American Journal of Sociology, published by the University of Chicago Press. Professor Small's views on the problems of profits are practically similar to those expressed by the English economist, Mr. Hobhouse. I will summarize them:
(1)	Stockholders should receive not more than a maximum rate of dividend calculated to be enougn above the average rate of return upon dividends to encourage investment in needed new industries.
(2)	Stockholders should be restrained from evading the prescribed dividend limitation by voting salar.es to themselves for services, mostly imaginary.
1.3) Premiums in the form of pro rata dividends on salaries and wages should be offered as inducements to increased output.
(4)	Net profits in excess of the prescribed dividends and premiums offered on salaries and wages should be divided in some proportion to be determined by experience between employees of all sorts and the state.
(5)	The state's share of the profits should not be available for governmental expenses, but should go to some holding concern, perhaps an adaptation of the Federal Reserve Bank, to be loaned to most desirable industrial enterprises-desirable from the standpoint not of private but of public interest.
I cannot altogether give my assent to all the proposals of this learned gentleman, but I refer them to the minister among others that he is going to take into his consideration.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
May I ask my hon. friend if
he does not think that already Canada takes a considerable share of the profits of these companies by way of income and other taxes?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I find some difficulty in arriving at a complete answer to that extraordinary question. I do
5 p.m. not think the government is taking anything like the income tax it should, either from individuals of from companies. I am in favour of a much more steeply graduated income tax than we have at the present time, and the elimination of indirect taxation altogether.
In conclusion, let me say that I sincerely trust the hon. member who introduced this resolution will see to it that the House gets an opportunity to vote upon it. I am anxious that that should be done in order that hon. gentlemen opposite will have an opportunity of registering themselves fairly on this question. I dislike very much to have them one session declaiming loudly against the evils of watered stock, and in the next session, anxious to avoid a vote upon it. We have, for example, the eloquent member for L'Islet (Mr. Fafaxd) who in discussing this whole question, at page 1714 of Hansard of last year said:
When the manufacturer bewails the fate of the poorly paid workmen, to justify a request for higher protection, he lacks sincerity; for when certain companies were realizing, during the war, profits of 25, 50 and even 100 per cent, the manufacturers did not idise the salary of the workman; on the contrary they even increased their capital fourfold in " watered stock " so as not to show too large a dividend.
I am quite sure the hon. member for L'Islet will be glad to vote for this resolution. Then we have that very eloquent gentleman the
Watered Stock

hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain). He took almost two whole pages of Hansard last year condemning the practice of amalgamation of companies for the purposes of issuing watered stock, and he quoted at some length-Hansard, page 1886- from the Montreal Financial Times dated April 11, 1924 showing how brazenly these corporations blazen forth their vast profits on the pages of the public journals. Then we have the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Putnam), who was perhaps one of the most outspoken on this matter. He says:
If dividends are doubled by the application of protection, the owners of the industry will resort to the very common device of watered stock in order to conceal from the consumer the extent to which he is exploited.
I notice my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Martell) has fled. I wonder is it because he is bored with the subject, or because he finds so many on his side are in favour of the abolition of watered stock? Why, I even find the Minister of Justice (Mr. La.pointe) speaking on the same subject. He does not attack the thing very pointedly, but he talks of watered stock mandarins, whatever a "mandarin" is, something very ferocious, a sort of bogey we are supposed to see in the woods, but which he never sees when he has a chance to invade them.
I therefore sincerely trust that the hon. member for Mackenzie will see to it that the hon. Minister of Justice and all his colleagues get an opportunity of voting on this question.

The hon. member states
that he would like the question put to a vote, in order that the government might place itself on record with regard to the question. Does he not think the easiest way out of the difficulty would be for the government to accept the resolution and put it in the waste-paper basket to-morrow?

speechtext:
I have no
doubt if they accept the resolution that danger would still be ahead of it, but I am willing to take the Secretary of State's word that he will accept the resolution and bring down the legislation upon it, and I am willing to wait.
I am always reasonable.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was indeed interested in the outlining of this subject by the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Copp). From the fact that his department has given this subject so very much consideration, I feel sure that the government as a whole will support the resolution as it is presented. Possibly when he was 
speaking he was thinking of the clause in the Speech from the Throne which referred to the tremendous high cost of living and the necessity of something being done to lower that cost. In my opinion, possibly no better steps could be taken than some drastic measure with regard to the control of the watering of stock. If this were done it would do more to cut down the high cost of living than many other things we could mention. We have to admit that the matter of centralization of industries is a most natural law in the development of civilization, but there is no reason why we should not regulate these industries, particularly with regard to this matter. There is no doubt, as other hon. gentlemen have said, that the matter of watering of stock brings many evils in its trail, and amongst others is the creating of a higher cost of living, the cutting down of purchasing power. It is one reason for the great labour unrest, and also for the vast unempl 03-men t we have at the present day. As the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) state, there is not the slightest doubt that the trouble we are having in Nova Scotia at the present time with the British Empire Steel Corporation is very largely brought about by this evil. The question of watered stock touches every industry, every trade and every life in this country, and it is not surprising therefore, to find the following resolution passed by a convention in Alberta:
Whereas, what is commonly known as watered stock is largely responsible for the high cost of living.
Therefore, be it resolved, that legislation be enacted prohibiting this practice.

Then it is just as well, as far as any light on the subject from the government side of the House is concerned. I have some opinions on the question. I do not think they are in agreement with any opinions offered so far-at least not in total agreement-but I shall present them to the House, in case they might be considered of some value by someone. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) opened with an expression of deep sympathy for the government benches, in that they found themselves perforce silent on a question on which their enthusiasm just a short time ago knew no bounds at all. My sympathy really is with hon. friends to my left, that the hopes with which they looked forward to great drastic reforms on this question of watered stock, as on many others, are dashed to the ground. I of course compliment them on the placidity, the good nature with which they meet the situation. That is, for the most part; some
of them seem to chafe under it, but others are more anxious to see that no Liberal opposes them in the next contest than they are to advance very far in the reforms they so long had at heart.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
What has that to do with
watered stock?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Watered stock had a lot to do with the same question a few years ago, but watered stock sinks into insignificance beside the stock that is not watered, in this House. We all remember not only the speech referred to by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) but the speeches of members of the present government themselves-yes, I have a very vivid recollection of the valiant attacks of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). He was a swordsman of wonderful skill, out in search of the big interests and these manipulators of watered stock; he was excelled only by the Prime Minister himself. But the cohorts were numerous, and this chamber used to ring with condemnation of the scandalous stock issues that were going out from the Secretary of State's office, and the whole practice of crushing the masses under this burden of overcapitalization.
The matter is brought up now by an hon. member to my left who has not forgotten his early training and beliefs. The hon. member presents the evils under which the people suffer, and he brings in a most moderate resolution for some sort of relief, doubtless in the hope that it would be accepted by the government. He asks them to do whatever is possible to alleviate the situation. The Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) representing the government replies, and I think I can give a synopsis of his reply. He admits that this is a very important question. He is pleased that it has been brought forward by the hon. gentleman of the Progressive party. He explains that it has caused a great deal of worry to himself and his officials. They have thought over it by day and slept over it by night. There are many phases to the question. Indeed, there are many kinds of watered stock. Some watered stock, he says, is given in payment of good will; other watered stock is given in payment of something else, so that there are different kinds of watered stock to complicate the situation, and thereby add to the difficulties of the administration. He ends, however, with the very momentous pledge, that this resolution moved by the hon. member will be placed by him before the officials of his department. Thus is represented the interest the government now has in the question of watered stock. The only sug-
Watered Stock

gestion the minister made was that he was ready to do this honour to the hon. gentleman's resolution-he was ready to find it a secluded sepulchre.
I said in opening that I am not in full accord with hon. gentlemen to my left on this question. I do not think that all they attribute to watered stock is directly or logically attributable to it. I am against the practice of issuing watered stock and in favour of its curtailment, for the reason that it is, on its face and in essence, a misrepresentation. There is only one kind of watered Stock, as everybody knows. What is meant by watered ' stock is watered stock issued for nothing. That is all. It is not watered stock issued for goodwill, but it is watered stock issued above the value of the goodwill, if for goodwill. In a word, all watered stock is issued for nothing and the public are invited to assume that it is worth its face value.
Before stating further the objections that I have to watered stock, let me refer to one or two allegations made by hon. gentlemen to my left. They seem to assume that watered stock forms the basis of a vested right to tariff protection. I take a position of direct opposition to any such assumption. I do not think watered stock forms any right whatever or constitutes any portion of any right to tariff protection. Nor, for ithat matter, do I think any stock constitutes in itself any portion of a right to tariff protection. Tariff protection does not rest on the need of paying dividends on stock. Tariff protection rests on the need of making a country and on nothing more. When hon. gentlemen lightly use the words that "the public are called upon to pay," I ask:	Who calls upon them to pay?
No government has a right to call upon them to pay and I do not know who there is besides a government. The public are not called upon to pay a nickel upon watered stock, or, for that matter, upon any stock. The public are absolutely free to pay or not to pay as they may see fit. Hon. gentlemen may say:	But a company gets into a position
where it has a monopoly of the field, and an instance is given of the Canada Cement Company. I am not saying that the Canada Cement Company is in that position; but if a company gets into the position of a monopoly, it does not get there because it has issued watered stock. It would be there just the same if it issued stock only to the value of the assets it possessed.

speechtext:
The contention that I
made was that the company by amalgamation of competing companies was in a position thereby to raise its prices.
[Mr. Meighen.l

speechtext:
Very good. If such is
the case, that unjust power of the company is due to the amalgamation and not to the fact that upon the amalgamation it issued watered stock. If upon amalgamation the Canada Cement Company had issued stock only to the exact value of even one-half the value of the property that went in, it would be none the less an amalgamation and it would hold just as great an area of Canada as its market.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Watered stock is a
result, not a cause of the merger.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Watered stock is only
an incident and has no relation to the power of the company after the amalgamation.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Is it not true that
companies refuse to pay higher wages on the ground that they cannot pay their dividends, those dividends being on watered stock?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
As I know companies,
they will not pay any more wages than they can avoid paying whether their stock is watered or not, nor will anybody else. They will pay the wages that they find they have to, first of all in the labour market and second, that will appear fairly satisfactory to the men employed. The question of the water in the company cannot be used logically by any concern. To my mind, no wage earner is so ignorant as to be in the slightest imposed upon by any company which urges the fact that it has to pay a dividend on watered stock, as a reason why it cannot pay wages.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Some boards are
so ignorant that they allow that to weigh with them in granting their awards.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
If any board of conciliation is, it ought to surrender its charter. I cannot conceive of any board of conciliation so ignorant as that. In a word, the fact of the water gives a company no right whatever, not even an ostensible, plausible right in respect of wages or tariff or anything else. It is argued as well that the issue of large blocks of watered stock has the effect of deceiving the public. In this, I am in full agreement. It is certainly true that to give a certificate on its face value which it does not possess is very likely to deceive, or contributes at least to deceiving the intending purchaser. Therein I find the main objection to the issue of stock that can be said at all to be watered.
I am aware that especially in this country as a confederation many difficulties present themselves in remedying the situation The

Watered Stock
provinces, as well as the Dominion, have the right to incorporate companies. The Dominion, upon its incorporation, has rights in respect of the control of capitalization of all kinds and the sale of stock representing the capitalization. It has no corresponding rights at all in respect of companies incorporated by a province. This Dominion incorporated most of the companies referred to by bon. members to my left. It incorporated the Canada Cement Company. It incorporated Ames-Holden. I think. It did not incorporate the British Empire Steel Corporation; that privilege was left for the government of Nova Scotia. But most of the companies complained of by hon. gentlemen to my left were incorporated federally, and whatever may be the responsibility for the issue of overcapitalization, it must rest on the government responsible for the issue of the letters of incorporation. But to the best of my recollection, every single one of the companies mentioned by hon. gentlemen to my left was incorporated either under this administration or under the administration which preceded 1911. It is a fact that all these mergers about which we have heard so much, the evils of which were crushing the population, were created one and all just a few years ago under the auspices and the authority of hon. gentlemen opposite or of their predecessors in the government of the Liberal party.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
tell the House why the charter of the Besco Company was refused by the federal government?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That could be done better by the hon. member who sits to my left (Sir Henry Drayton). However, I will give a frank answer. The application was made; it was held in the office of the Department of Finance for many weeks; and the charter was withheld on the ground that in the judgment of the department the capitalization issue was too high. It was finally withdrawn by the company itself; and no absolute, written refusal having been given, application was made to the government of Nova Scotia and a charter was issued in pursuance thereof.
I was going to make some reference to the companies mentioned by hon. gentlemen to my left. Let me say again, as I sand before, that the actual incorporation of these companies, irrespective of the capitalization, gave them no right whatever to any tariff protection. In a word, the right to tariff protection does not rest upon the necessities of any concern at all; tariff protection is not in any way whatever an individual right. Tariff
protection is a matter of policy, and the only question before a government or parliament is-is it better for the nation? It is not a question whether protection is needed by any corporation or individual.
Reference has been made repeatedly to the great amount of water injected into the stock issue of the Canada Cement Company. I do not think it can be reasonably disputed that this allegation is correct. Certainly, however, I was in no way, nor was any one of my political friends, responsible for its issue. I think it is a fact that that company to-day controls a very large share of the market of this country; I suppose it has reached perhaps the proportions of as large a controllable market as any single concern in Canada. Hon. gentlemen to my left as well as hon. members opposite used to inveigh against that condition of affairs; and they threatened that as respects the commodity produced by this particular concern there was going to be free entry into this Dominion after they came into power. Now, I may tell hon. gentlemen to my left, confidentially that I do not think that anything I could say would persuade hon. gentlemen opposite to interfere with the tariff on cement. But I do not want anything I Shall say to indicate that it is my view that Canada suffers to-day because of the tariff on cement. I do not think it does. I believe it is a fact that to-day cement sells lower in this country than in the United States or in any of our competing countries. That I believe is true. I know there is a great deal of watered stock, but I do not think that those who suffer are the public of Canada. There doubtless are sufferers, I presume; but they are not, I say, the Canadian public. I have made that statement because I have no wish to appear as the defender of this concern; I do not need to defend it. As I said before, no appeal however fervent, nor any language however eloquent, on my part would have any effect on hon. gentlemen opposite in this respect.
The question comes, then, as to what can be done in this country under the difficulties I have mentioned incident to our federal system. We cannot control the issue of provincial charters. If we placed restrictions on the issue of federal charters which would give less rights to the companies applying federally, then they could apply provincially, the probable result would be that the number of provincial charters would be increased -while the federal charters would diminish. What could be done would be mainly by co-operation with the provinces. And even then care would have to be taken that the restrictions were not such as might give to the incorpor-
Watered Stock

atoTS in other countries, who would operate here under license, any advantage over Canadian concerns. I have always felt, and subject to any further light I can get on the question, I still feel, that there is no reason why stocks should have any par value at all. I do not know why the state should put its imprimatur on any special value attributable to a certificate of stock. Some years ago, I think a couple of years before the late government went out, we introduced and , put through parliament an amendment to the Companies Act to provide for the issue of stock of no par value. Many companies have since been incorporated on that basis; their stock has no par value at all and therefore no one can be deceived. But of course the company still has the right to get stock and fix a par value if it applies. I presume that most of the applicants still ask for the issue of stock of regular par value, and if we ourselves were to proceed to limit the grants of charters to those who issued only stock of no par value, unless the provinces did likewise, it might result in a larger number of provincial issues and a withdrawal to a degree from the federal field. But if the provinces would concur and would adopt the practice of issuing charters only in the case of stock of no par value, it seems to me that a better state of affairs would ensue. No purchaser of the stock could be deceived by anything the government did. He might still be deceived by the seductions of agents; he might still be deceived by misrepresentation on the part of the company. But at least this parliament could be certain that he would not be deceived by a nominal par value across the face of a certificate, placed there on the authority of the government acting by virtue of a statute. This it seems to me would be a real reform. I have never seen advanced any reason that appealed to me at all, why the state should be asked to fix any special par value on a certificate of stock. And this in my judgment applies to preferred stock just as much as to common stock. As respects all that represents the proprietary interest in any concern, why should the state decide what the face value of a certificate is?
There would still remain the problem of controlling the sale of the stock even though it issued without par value. This cannot be done by the federal parliament alone. The federal parliament can control in the first place the sale of stock of companies enjoying federal charters; that is to say, the sale by the company itself. But we could not control the sale by those who purchased from the companies, in whatever form they might purchase.
[Mr. Meighen.j
Similarly, the provinces alone can control the sale in the first place of stock that issues from provincial companies but not the subsequent sale of stock after it has passed from the hands of the company itself. The different provinces have sought to effect such control; the first was Manitoba under the regime of the Roblin government. The blue sky law which that government put through the legislature was in my judgment most efficacious. At the time of the gas and oil boom of about thirteen years ago it saved innocent purchasers in that province hundreds of thousands if not millions of dollars. I do not know whether it is in effect now or not; until the Solicitor General intervened I was under the impression that it had been allowed to die.

speechtext:

I do think that every encouragement should be given-and it is probable that legislative restrictions to that end could be imposed-I do think that every encouragement should be given to the issue of stock of no par value, and that an effort should be made to secure the co-operation of the provinces to adopt a like policy. If all did so, then there could be no misrepresentation under federal or provincial sanction, and

Watered Stock
at the same time there would be no impoverishment of the powers of a company which would handicap it as compared with its competitors in other lands which might operate under license here. Let me say that I think a reform can be effected. I do not oppose the resolution at all. What I rose mostly to do was to declare my conviction that the extent of the reform is not half as great as the mass of people imagine, and the extent of the evil is not at all that portrayed !by many who have spoken in this debate. It seems to me that we have far more watered stock to-day, Mr. Speaker, than we had a few years ago. Watered stock is stock that represents no value. What may be represented by water alone one day, may be represented by value a few years after; what may be represented by value one day may be represented by water a few years after. So water is not injected only on the incorporation; the water is the result of the process of time, of management, and of public policy, and the stock issues of thousands of companies which had par value, and for which full value was given, are to-day represented by nothing: they are water pure and simple and the water itself has evaporated. It is of far more concern to this parliament to see to it that we follow a policy which gives value to the operations of concerns, and thereby gives some value to their stock. It is far more important that we direct our attention to these things than that, we worry over evils which to a large extent are imaginary, and which in any event at the present time are beyond our power to cure except to a small extent.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree altogether with what the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) has said in regard to this resolution. But I would go a bit further and make a suggestion to the government, especially to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr Robb), that the way to get at the evil is through the income tax; and the income tax is with us now to Siay for a good many years. If a company is found to be taking unfair advantage of the people, and I do not care how much watered stock is in it, I would subject its assets and its business to strict examination. If it is found to be taking unfair profits by reason of watered stock, let it be punished by increasing the income tax. In other words, have a flexible, adjustable income tax. The Pullman Car Company of Chicago is verv heavily capitalized now. They know they are taking too much out of the public in their sleeper charges, and half of their profits now go back to the railway companies. I take it
that the Canadian National is drawing an immense income from the contract that the old Grand Trunk had with the Pullman Company. Another great company over-capitalized is the Standard Oil Company, and they are making restitution to the public through ihe Rockefeller family, who have made enormous charitable donations for various public purposes. But the greatest over-capitalization in history is in process of formation in the United States, where the consolidation is being formed of all the telegraph companies, the Bell Telephone Company, and the cable and wireless companies, and the flotation will be made almost any day. There should be a way of getting at these companies, and the only way I see is to measure up the service they give against the income they receive from the public, and tax their enormous profits. As the leader of the opposition says, there are lots of companies that are no good now, and there is no reason why the public should continue to be taxed, even if Max Aitken did get a peerage because he floated a great deal of watered stock on the Canadian people. There is the example that is set up for all the boys of Canada to-day: Pe a Max Aitken and then you will become a peer in England.
You cannot punish the men who float these mergers, but you can make them share their over-profits with the public. The Acting Minister of Finance is looking for further income, and perhaps he and the Secretary of State will accept my suggestion. Let them get some " mousers " to find out how these excessive profits can be taxed. I want to toll him what takes place in the province of Ontario. There when estates are valued for probate, and the mouser they have up there in the attorney general thinks the valuations are too low, he checks them up and sees that a fair amount of the estate comes to tlic province by payment of higher duties. The Acting Minister of Finance is very much in need of increased revenue and he should devise such a scheme as this. The responsibility is not on private members to apply a cure, it is on him and on the government, and I hope instead of following the mild suggestion of the Secretary of State-he says to the House, "If you give us some suggestion we will follow it up "-I hope instead of following this course the government will lealize that the duty is on them to frame a policy to protect the investor. The only way I can see of effecting this is to adopt more and more the principle of no par value stock Let every one of these companies be investigated each year so that their assets and their profits may be accurately determined, regard-
Watered Stock

less of the amount of watered stock there may be. They have no right to say that watered stock is entitled to a dividend and that before any tax can be imposed upon it the dividend must be paid. That is not the issue at all. It is the income of the company that ought to be taxed. The only way to get at the difficulty, especially where a company's in-< come is based either upon a monopoly or upon watered stock, is to investigate the company every year; you will put the fear of God into them if they have to make an annual statement. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is going to vote on this; I want to tell him to get a mouser in his department and we will find out about these things. That is the only way to get rid of this grievance-and it is a grievance-with respect to watered stock. There are more victims of watered stock in this country than of anything else. As the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) says, the provinces and the Dominion must agree on this matter; we must have a united policy. But even that will not work out as effectively as the method I have just suggested. If you find a company making exorbitant profits, then they must know that they are not entitled either to the protection of the tariff or to protection in respect to their watered stock, to the extent that dividends must be paid on that stock before the public are protected.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not think there could be any two opinions as to what watered stock is. To me the whole thing has a moral aspect apart from its economic side. There is no doubt that in the years past companies and promoters have capitalized the benefits granted to them by politicians in both the Dominion and the provincial legislatures, such as tariffs, bonuses, bounties, subsidies, tax exemptions, land grants and so on. Watered stock in capitalization is really an American feature, and I think it reached its peak in Canada during the administration of the Laurier government some years ago. To me the whole thing is a fraudulent abstraction of money from the pockets of the people. The representatives of the people, therefore, are entirely responsible for the whole thing. It does really amount in the end to a sale of the rights of the people, to giving the right to certain promoters to take money out of the pockets of the consumers and wage earners of this country. In a speech made in this House on March 22, 1892, Sir Richard Cartwright said:
Thousands of dollars were turned over at Red Parlour conferences to those who devised robbery for the development, of the election fund.
fMr. W. F. Maclean.]
There is not a doubt in my mind that corruption is a part of the National Policy itself; that the National Policy tends to corruption of politicians. Indeed, Sir, the Labour Herald of Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, December 6, 1924, has this to say regarding the British Empire Steel Corporation:
Some time before parliament adjourned Mr. Joe Steel, M.P.P., asked several questions in regard to the purchase of coal by the government for public buildings. Below we give the reply which he received. Study the prices paid to the different companies. Look at Inverness : bankrupt Inverness, gets as low as $4.60 per ton for coal, and the British Empire Steel Corporation for coal not one whit better, and in some respects not so good, receives $11.75. Why the difference of $7.15? There is only one answer: The British Empire Steel Corporation buys up governments, and politicians are for sale. No politician would ever look to bankrupt Inverness to finance his election or other expenses. But Besco can do it, and did it in Newfoundland. And where does Besco get the money to spend on corrupt politicians? Out of the public with the consent of the politicians.
Canada stands well up in the list to-day as an exploiting capitalistic country. From an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of June 29, 1924, I clipped the following:
The manufacturing of millionaires has been frequently mentioned, and recently there has been publicity added regarding the increase of inflated wealth through various corporation mergers. The formation of this one steel corporation is an excellent example of the prevailing method of "making" money.	_
The authorized statements of the corporation provide the facts. The projected financial statement published over the name of the president discloses the fact than the liability for bonds and debenture stock, representing the intrinsic value of the properties, amounts to $31,102,000, to which must be added deferred payments of $1,484,000. There has been issued in addition to the foregoing $101,750,000, and so far as evidence appears in this regard, this amount appears to be entirely in the nature of a bonus distribution to the bondholders and the parties promoting the merger. The issuing of this large amount of liability of over $100,000,000 is easily balanced by a book entry, as in the case of the British company.
On the asset side of the statement the "land, buildings, plant, machinery, mining properties, and equipment" is written up to $130,000,000 by simply adding to the bonded indebtedness of $31,000,000 the $101,000,000 of common and preferred stock. That this appears to be an exact statement of the facts is confirmed by data taken from Poor and Moody's Manual Consolidated for 1922. The old issues of the merging companies amounted to $63,000,000 common and $19,000,000 preferred. The merger transformed this into $24,000,000 common and $77,000,000 preferred, thus adding to the previous inflated capital the sum of $19,000,000 by way of still further inflation.
So there can. be no doubt that to-day the British Empire Steel Corporation-and I say this in answer to the hon. member for Hants- (Mr. Martel!)-are squeezing their employees to pay a dividend on this watered stock.
Again, perhaps Dominion Canners Limited will furnish a good example of the watered stock method of robbing the consumers of Canada. That is one of the greatest evils

Watered Stock
of the protectionist system of this country. Some 43 companies amalgamated under the name of Dominion Canners Limited. This I take from an issue of the Farmers Sun of November 26, 1921. The actual capitalization of the various companies merged was $115,-
442,000.	They were authorized to issue exactly double the amount of stock, or $230,-
884,000.	Surely the responsibility must rest heavily on those who granted them this privilege.
Watered stock is essentially and particularly a feature of a protected nation. No doubt it is practised in some other countries, but as the Secretary of State said, the stock does have some value there in purchasing goodwill and the like; but here on this continent no value whatsoever seems to be given, and that is how the name of water has come to be used in this connection, because water really represents no value.
I need go no further to show the evils of the system, because my colleagues have already proved the existence of watered stock in the capitalization of many concerns. Some bon. gentlemen in this House are forever crying for more protection; but here is one feature of class privilege that is destroying even the industrial concerns whom it was supposed to benefit. We have built up the industrial concerns of this country on a plan on which it is now really impossible for them to compete. The hon. leader of the opposition declares that 2,000 of these factories have had to close their doors; he says be can vouch for the truth of this. But this is only what may be expected of all that are left before our industries come to run on a rock-bottom basis. It is not possible for an exporting country like Canada, for a country that derives most of its income from the export of agricultural products to ever carry on on this artificial basis. There is really only one industry in Canada that is paying its way to-day, and that is agriculture; and this industry has been bled for the last forty years for the sake of over-capitalized concerns. It is doubtful indeed if under the tariff system and watered stock capitalization we have not paid more in that way than even the total amount that has been paid by these industries in wages during all this time.
