speechtext:
The hon. member can take the floor after I have finished, and show this

Watered Stock

statement not to be a fact, if it is possible. Let us consider this fact: that during the war when there was a prospect of wheat being high in price and the farmer had a chance of meeting the profiteering of the factory owners and distributors, the government arrested the price of wheat. It was stabilized then at about fifty per cent of what it ought to have been, and What the price would likely have been, while the manufacturers of munitions and supplies of war were permitted, by their faithful representatives in this House, to sky-rocket their charges and mulct this Dominion to the extent of the two billions of dollars that represents the public debt. Now the agriculturist and wage earner are supposed to pay this debt, a thing they did not incur, while the manufacturer goes free from paying even a fractional part, because he is still enabled by protection and watered stock to pass on his just debts to the wealth producer. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the debt of this country belongs to the watered stock companies and not to the agriculturist who had the price of his product fixed by law. When deflation started the price of wheat was not kept at the stabilized price set by the government until all the other commodities that entered into the cost of living and production came down to that level, but wheat along with all the other farm products, including live stock, was the first to fall in prices. During all the time since the war'closed the government has stood by and has been content to let all the watered stock bear dividends by further fleecing the agriculturist. Even the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which has in the past divided melons of sixty and ninety million dollars among shareholders, were allowed to sky-rocket their rates so that ten per cent might be paid on hundreds of millions that they never invested in that concern. I say, Sir, that Canadian industries and public utilities will have to be drained of their water. It is time some idea of justice and equity prevailed in business throughout this Dominion, so that the different classes in the Dominion might have some confidence in each other and that the sectional differences of the country created by favouritism, class privilege and corruption, may be equalized before it is too late. It is useless at this time to talk of unity and optimism while these sores on the body politic exist, while parliament, instead of meeting out even-handed justice, is yet a place where privilege is dispensed.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a reference or two to the remarks delivered this after-

noon. I was rather surprised to hear the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) make the statement that people did not have to buy from these corporations. I should like to ask the Secretary of State if he would put that question to the citizens of Ottawa or to the citizens of Winnipeg or to the municipal council of any municipality, if they do not have to buy cement from the Canada Cement Company, or, if they buy from any other company, if they do not have to pay the price fixed by the Canada Cement Company, because that company absolutely controls the market to-day. Let me quote a little instance. On July 8, 1909, the city of Winnipeg purchased 25,000 barrels of cement which they secured at $1.77 per barrel. That was just before the merger took place. Three months later, after the merger was formed, they called for tenders for a smaller quantity. They received only three tenders each of them from an agent of the Canada Cement Company. They received tenders from no other company and the lowest price at which they could secure the cement was $2,24 a barrel. It is useless to ask the citizens of Winnipeg if they cannot buy the cement somewhere else and in that way avoid paying interest or dividends on watered stock.
Ask the people of Canada from the Atlantic to -the Pacific if they can avoid buying their oil, gasoline or fuel oil from the Standard Oil Company, because, after all, every oil company that is doing business in Canada to-day, I care not what be its name, depends entirely upon the Standard Oil Company. There is really no competition in the oil business in Canada at the present time. It is controlled by that one company.
Ask the farmers of the northwest why they use the vessels of the Canada Steamship Company, why the}'- provide business for that company. They have no alternative. The government of this country in putting a prohibitive rate on our railways to the sea prevents us from shipping our wheat to a logical point that would be a competing point for these vessels and forces us to hand it over to them whether we wish it or not. As usual, a great mass of legal difficulties is placed in the way of something being done. I have always found, since I have been in this House, that wherever something requires to be done for the common people, there is no end of legal difficulty in the way, the thing is impossible to overcome. But when one of the corporations needs something, these difficulties all seem to disappear immediately. When it was necessary to start the Canadian Pacific, to give it grants, cash subsidies, 25,-

Watered Stock
000.000 acres of free land, there were no legal difficulties. The provincial governments, where these lands were situated, did not have to be consulted. The whole thing went through without any trouble. It all depends, to use the old and perhaps a little vulgar saying, whose ox is being gored.
The Canadian Northern came to this parliament in financial difficulties in 1917. If the government of that day had not wanted to deal with the matter, they could have placed any number of legal difficulties in the way of providing means for the Canadian Northern to carry on. They got over those difficulties. The difficulties automatically vanished, because this was a huge corporation looking for something. The government of that day started the printing presses running and they printed about $25,000,000 of money which they handed over to that company. I am not particularly criticizing the government of that day. In fact, I think they did right. It was necessary to do something quickly. But when the people of this country want something, when the farmers are in distress, when the working people of Nova Scotia are in trouble, there seems to be none of that statesmanship that was shown on that particular occasion.

speechtext:
I think my responsibility ends when I place before the government the necessity for legislative and administrative action. The responsibility for that action is then entirely on the government. The members of the government are more interested in avoiding embarrassment for the administration than in meeting the situation and trying to secure a remedy for it. The hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches must accept that responsibility. They cannot continually invite suggestions from this side of the House. We give them suggestions, but the responsibility is on them to provide legislation. The Solicitor General (Mr. McMur-ray) invited some suggestions from the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth), and I could not help thinking that if the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg were in the position of the Solicitor General, he would not be asking anybody on this side of the House for suggestions to deal with the situation, he would deal with it fearlessly, courageously and actually do something. That is what the people of this country want today. They want to see on the government benches men who are attempting something and not simply marking time. The confession of any government of inability to deal with a situation of this kind is simply a confession of inability to carry on the government itself.
We have been discussing for a long time, a contract known as the Petersen agreement, the object of which is supposed to be the control of a combine. The government are making, or at least they think they are making, some attempt to deal with that situation, of which there is no doubt a good deal of political capital will be made in the country. They will appeal for popular support on the ground of what they are trying to do, whether the measure passes the House or not. Well, here is a combine that has existed for generations, and so far nothing effective has been done to control it. Here is an opportunity for the government to show itself to the country a real combine-smashing administration. If they take effective steps to cope with this evil they will have something tangible to show the country.
Watered Stock

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) a few nights ago declared that we must line up either for or against the combine. That is precisely what I want to see, and an excellent opportunity presents itself right now for hon. gentlemen in all parts of the chamber to line up either for or against a dangerous combine. All sorts of obstacles are placed before us, however; legal impediments are suggested; and the British North America Act is again brought forward. It seems to me that those hon. gentlemen who raise the British North America Act now as a legal difficulty which we cannot get over should have supported the resolution of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) a few days ago when he proposed a means of meeting that difficulty. But I am not particularly concerned about that act. When there are on the treasury benches gentlemen who have the will to control watered stock, regardless of the British North America Act, such control will be brought about. It is only two years ago since the same legal difficulties were conjured up when it was proposed to institute a system of inspecting banks. Hon. gentlemen at that time said it could not be done and that statement was echoed all through the House; the whole atmosphere of government was filled with the same thing-it simply cannot be done. But we did it; it is a fact to-day.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Who did it?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CAMPBELL FOR RESTRICTIVE LEGISLATION
speechtext: The government; but the government did it only when forced into action by public opinion. The government simply rode like a chip on the crest of a wave instead of directing the course of that wave. Now, I want to see on the government benches gentlemen who will direct these waves instead of being forced into a certain position by the trend of public opinion. We are controlling the insurance companies, for we have an officer with supervisory powers to keep in touch with them. We are also controlling our railways, and we are overseeing the banks. There is therefore no logical reason why the government should not exercise some control over the issue of watered stock. All that is needed is the will to action on the part of those in power.

I stand corrected. I refer
to the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). We have so many members from Toronto that we may be pardoned. Sir, if we sometimes do not designate them rightly. This editorial is headed, "Reduce the duty on motors," and proceeds:
Whatever else may be done with the customs tariff at the next session of parliament, there should be a substantial reduction in the duty on motor cars. It is clear from the prices quoted in the United States and Canada that the Canadian manufacturers are charging " all the traffic will stand." The duty of 35 per cent is more than protection. It is in part a government subsidy to the makers of automobiles. As long as the motor car was purely a luxury that only the rich could enjoy, there was not much reason for complaint. But the motor car has become a necessity in business and professional life, and those who are thus compelled to buy one should not be forced to pay excessive profits to the manufacturers. A certain type of car that sells in the United States at $1,875, costs $3,100 in Canada. That is altogether too wide a sjpread, and is not warranted by any factor in the trade. The American makers have larger production, it is true, but they pay higher wages, and there is no reason why their raw materials are any cheaper. The makers of motor cars in Canada are soaking the public unduly, and it is the duty of the government to lower the tariff, and in that way inject a little competition of American firms that will bring down the prices.
This editorial is from the Orange Sentinel of November 6, 1923. I have one other quotation which I should like to read in this connection. It is from the June number of the Textile Journal, a copy of which I think was sent to all the members of this House. It
contains a plea from a great many manufacturers for more tariff protection, and this is the way that one manufacturer puts the case. He says:
We presume manufacturers in every line-
He is asking for more protection.
-with the possible exception of the automobiles, in which we think there is an exorbitant protection, are suffering along the same lines.
Wherever men are gathered together in this country to discuss matters of current interest the tariff is very likely to be one of the topics engaging their attention, and you will always find many supporters of a protective tariff policy, but when autpmobiles are mentioned almost unanimously it will be agreed that the duty is much too high. I believe that the figures respecting the export of automobiles will prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that our motor manufacturers should now be able to get along with a substantial reduction of the protection they are enjoying.

Another reason why there should be a reduction in the duty is that the prices of automobiles and trucks in Canada to-day are not based on the cost of production. The automobile manufacturers are basing their prices in Canada on the United States price plus the duty of 35 per cent. It should be noted that there is an excise tax of 5 per cent in the United States and when our customs officials collect the duty on imported cars they add the 5 per cent excise tax to the sale price in the United States and use that as the value for duty purposes. This in reality makes the duty approximately 37 per cent of the price in the United States. There is in Canada in addition a sales tax of 5 per cent based on the duty paid value of the car and an excise tax of 5 per cent on the duty paid value up to $1,200 and 10 per cent upon any value in excess of $1,200. I would now like to make a few remarks in regard to the duty on second hand cars which Canadians sometimes import from the United States. I took this matter up with the Department of Customs and in a memorandum which they prepared for me on the subject of used cars they state:
Used motor cars are subject to appraisal at the time and place of importation according to the condition of the imported cars. The practice of appraisers is to base the valuation on the list price of corresponding current models of imported cars and, under average conditions, to allow discounts for depreciation as follows:
Cars listed at less than $1,000 1 year's use	25 per cent
Mr. Speaker, you can go to the United States and buy these cars at a depreciation of 50 per cent. Why should the customs authorities take it upon themselves to arbitrarily say: No matter what you paid for this car you are going to pay duty on the basis of the list price of the car less depreciation of 25 per cent? On a car that has been in use two years they allow depreciation of 35 per cent; on a car in use for three years, 45 per cent; on a car that has been in use four years, 50 per cent. Now you can go to the United

States and secure a car that has had four years use at a depreciation of at least 80 per cent on the list price. On cars listed at $1,000 and over, after one year's use, 30 per cent depreciation is allowed. That should be at least 50 per cent. After two years use of the same car depreciation of 45 per cent is allowed; after three years use, 55 per cent; after four years use, 60 per cent.
Now you can get a used car costing originally $1,000 at a depreciation of from 80 to 90 per cent in the United States at any time, and anyone who will take the trouble to take an American newspaper and look at the advertisements for used cars will find that I have stated it conservatively.
I would like to give just two examples that have come under my notice of the valuation that has been placed on used cars by customs officers for duty purposes. In one case a Ford motor car was purchased in Spokane for $50 by two young men who were coming up to harvest in Alberta. When they got to the line the customs officer demanded $50 duty and tax on that car. They told him they had only paid $50 for the car and did not intend to pay $50 duty, and he could take the car.
The other case was of five young men coming up to harvest in Alberta who had a Chevrolet, 19201 model. I am sure that car could have been bought second-hand any place in the United States1 for $100 or less. They were required to pay $97 duty on that car. I am sure that statement is correct because I know these young men. As a matter of fact, when they got as far north as my place they were absolutely broke, and could not go any farther because they had no money to buy gas. They had to get work. It had taken all their money to pay the duty.
I feel this is a matter of very great importance to Canadians. A world car census recently made places Canada third in the number of cars used. The United States is first with 15,222,000 cars, or one car to about every seven people. Great Britain is second with
655,000,	and Canada third with 642,571, or one car to about fourteen people. With our sparse population scattered over such a large territory we need more motor cars and trucks. After all, Mr. Speaker, this is, I think, a question of transportation. Can we afford to pay 50 per cent more for our cars and trucks than the people of the United States? As a matter of fact, I believe this is one of the factors which is responsible for so many of our people having moved to the United States. People to-day are bound to have motor cars, and if they can get a motor car across the line for 50 per cent less than they have to pay here,

Tariff on Automobiles
other things being equal, they are very likely to go across the line. In many cases the price is prohibitive here, and they feel that if they go to the United States, where used cars particularly can be had very cheap, they will be able to enjoy the advantages of a car.
Transportation is one of the great-9 p.m. est questions confronting this country to-day. That is stated in the Speech from the Throne, and I take it that it must be a fact. Here is what the Ford Times says about one phase of this question:
The development of the automotive industry is only a logical sequence of the demand for transportation facilities, which have always played a major part in opening up a land to its fullest possibilities. With vast unopened areas in our land of huge distances, proper railroad service could not be a paying or a practical proposition. The need for transportation still remains and is of prime importance in changing these waste spaces into productive areas. No country can rise to its full height of importance without adequate transportation. Those who wonder at the continued increase in the sale of automobiles must realize that the big increases are in cars selling for less than $1,000. These constitute more than 80 per cent of the present market. Such cars are bought for their money-earning power. They earn their cost and keep. The automobile industry could never have attained its present tremendous totals over a period of 23 years had not its product more than justified itself economically. Its proper use lengthens life, increases efficiency, stimulates general business and promotes the wealth and stability of the nation.
Cars, Mr. Speaker, are a necessity for many people-doctors, merchants, travellers and I would also say many of our preachers, particularly in the western provinces, and more particularly our farmers. I have heard it. estimated that our farmers in Alberta live on an average about twelve miles from the railway station, but that not more than one-third of them have motor cars. This government has always been preaching to these people that they should engage in mixed farming. The government want these farmers to milk cows, and if the farmers are to milk the cows, as we have very few cheese factories in that country, the cream must be taken to the creamery or to the station. It should be taken at least twice a week, particularly in warm weather. The man who lives ten or twelve miles from the station and has to make two trips to town during the week, is going to lose two days off the land, if he has to drive a team, because he cannot make the trip in half a day. If he has a car he will likely take the cream can to town in the evening, after he has done his day's work. We have many farmers in the west who are hauling their grain twenty or twenty-five miles or even further to the railways stations.
When they used horses these men took two days to make the round trip to town and back. 1 want hon. members to consider what a task that is. They must go to the hotel at night, pay for a bed, and two meals, put their horses in a livery stable and pay a livery bill for them. But with a motor truck many of them can make two trips to town in one day. I was told that in one district in my constituency there were over twenty farmers this fall who were using motor trucks, most of them hauling their wheat twenty or twenty-two miles to the station. These men complained! that their trucks cost them practically fifty per cent more than they cost across the line. Do hon. gentle,men think these farmers are prosperous enough to be able to pay the increased price? With regard to this question Henry Ford says:
The great trouble with farming is that it involves too much unnecessary work. There is no reason why agriculture may not hope to come abreast of the other industries in the near future, if the farmer will turn his attention to modern industrial methods, instead of to the problem of borrowing money. There is no food scarcity. The problem is not one of how to increase production, and thereby pile up a surplus for speculators to play with, but how to simplify production and distribution so that less human energy shall be wasted in the process.
Thus is America's industrial genius quoted in a recent issue of Farm and Home.
This government has spent millions of dollars to get people on the land, and one trouble they have is that after they get people on the land many of them will not stay there. If there is orte thing more than another necessary to keep people on the land it is improved transportation facilities which implies liberty to purchase automobiles at a reasonable price. Here is another article taken from the Ford Times. It reads:
Autos Reduce The Farm Migration Easy to Get to Town Now; Just a Case of Starting the Family Car
The farm telephone, the coming of labour-saving devices and the low-priced auto are three of the greatest factors in checking the admittedly large migration from the farm.
I want to say a word particularly in behalf of the farm women. Many of these women living on a farm anywhere from ten to twenty miles from town live a very lonely life indeed, and I do not wonder that they leave their farms. The only wonder to me is that so many of them stay as long as they do. This article says:
Many a farm wife will testify that it has meant the disappearance of monotony, since in pre-auto days to get away meant harnessing up an already tired horse, with a limited radius. Now it is just a case of starting the family car, with a triple radius of possibility.
Tariff on Automobiles

As I said before, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be a very liberal estimate to say that one farmer out of three in the province of Alberta is able to own a motor car. The importance of this subject is demonstrated by the fact that we spent in the year 1923 in Canada probably a hundred million dollars in the purchase of automobiles and trucks. The value of cars manufactured in Canada for home consumption was $63,541,000 and the value of imported cars and trucks, $11,443,000, making a total of $74,984,000. If you would add to this the amount of duty paid on imported cars, the sales tax, excise tax and retail commission, it would probably run over one hundred million dollars. A reduction of ten per cent in the selling price of cars in Canada would make available ten million dollars of new purchasing power, which would be used to purchase more automobiles and more of the common necessities of life, and the taxation incident to the spending of that ten million dollars would bring in considerable revenue to the Finance department.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I presume that the question will be asked-I am a little surprised it has not been asked already-what are you going to do to make up the loss of revenue? Because there would be some loss of revenue. For the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1924, the duty on automobile parts not otherwise provided imported into Canada was $5,123,000, on engines $1,389,000, on rubber tires for vehicles of all kinds $351,000, giving a total of $6,864,000 duty collected on .automobile parts. Forty-seven per cent of the cars and trucks made in Canada were exported, so that you would deduct forty-seven per cent of this amount for drawbacks and that would give you an amount of $3,226,000. The total of drawbacks paid to automobile manufacturers was $5,223,000.
If you take off $3,226,000 drawback, that would leave a net balance of $3,637,000; then add to that the customs collected on motor cars, $3,316,000, and the customs collected on trucks, $661,000, and you have a total of $7,615,000.

speechtext: I understood the hon. member to say there would be a reduction in the revenue if the duty were decreased. Does he assume that there would be no greater number of importations than we have now, or does he think that it would follow that because there is a reduction in duty and consequently a reduction in the price of American cars, that the Canadian manufacturer would merely reduce his price and sell just as many cars?

maintopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF ON AUTOMOBILES AND MOTOR TRUCKS
speechtext: Sell more.

maintopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF ON AUTOMOBILES AND MOTOR TRUCKS
speechtext:
I would not anticipate any
greater importation of American cars. I think the Canadian manufacturer would reduce the price and we would buy Canadian cars just as we are doing now, and I may say I think it would be a good thing so far as general industry is concerned. I believe there would be more motor cars sold and more men employed in Canada than there are to-day in that particular industry. Supposing that a reduction of 17-J per cent even were made in the present tariff, there would apparently be a net loss of $3,807,000. The excise tax collected in 1904 was $2,689,399. Supposing we added 7^ per cent to the excise tax. This would give an increase in revenue of approximately $4,000,000, which would a little more than offset the loss of revenue by the reduction in the tariff if we made the same number of importations of foreign cars. You could thus reduce the price of automobiles 10 per cent without interfering in any way with our revenues through customs and excise.
Statistics for the year 1923 which I have here show that the value of cars manufactured in Canada in 1923 was $97,369,814. Deduct from that the value of passenger cars exported, $29,325,000 and the value of trucks exported $4,503,000, and you have a total manufactured value of cars consumed at home of $63,541,814. This value is about one-third more on account of the tariff of 35 per cent, or it actually works out at a little more than 35 per cent, as I tried to show earlier in my remarks. Let us assume that we paid $20,000,000 more for these cars on account of the duty. The number of men employed in the industry last year was 9,305 persons at an average wage of $1,600 and the total amount paid in wages was $14,998,000. Or in other words, we paid in increased prices on account of the tariff $5,000,000 more than the total salaries and wages paid by the industry. Is it good business for us to pay such a price for the establishment of this industry in Canada, or I should say, after the industry is established, should we continue to pay this price? After all, who is going to benefit from the tariff? The Ford Times of June 14, 1923 refers to the erection of its new plant at Ford, Ontario, in these words:
Hard by, the new $10,000,000 Ford factory is rapidly nearing completion and when the wheels of production start turning there, Canada can boast the largest automobile plant in the British Empire.
Canada does not own that plant. The bulk of the stock and bonds in that industry is owned in the United States. It is hard to get definite figures in regard to the percentage

Tariff on Automobiles
of capital in this industry controlled in Canada and in the United States, but the latest figures I have seen state that 80 per cent of the capital invested in this industry is owned in the United States. As I have shown in the case of at least one large company, it has all been built up out of earnings in Canada, yet it is largely owned now in the United States. In a clipping from the Financial Post of February 29, 1924, there is this statement:
Practically all the manufacturing plants in Canada are either branches of American factories or are controlled by American cap:+al their location in the Dominion enabling them to take advantage of the preferential tariff treatment in certain countries of the British Empire.
This is a little clipping also from the Post in regard to the Dodge Brothers plant being established in Canada:
Establishment of this plant overcomes the handicap in Canadian operations resulting from tariff requirements and enables the company to market its cars at prices more in line with those in the United States.
When I think of how we have bled ourselves for the benefit of these American millionaires, I am tempted to exclaim as did the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) a year ago: "How long, Oh, Lord, how long?"
I have here, I think it is an editorial originally printed in the Vancouver Sun, but it is reprinted in the Ford Times of Ford, Ontario. I presume when they reprint it in their editorial column they must approve it:
To-day, the purchasing power of the American dollar is 100 cents. Compared with the goods which that American dollar will buy in United States, our Canadian dollar, spent in Canada, will buy goods worth not more than 70 cents, and it makes no difference whether the purchase is an automobile, a pound of sugar, or a cotton dress.
I believe as regards automobiles I have proved that is the case. If the Ford Times published this editorial, surely they must approve the sentiments contained therein, and I do not believe they would seriously object to a reduction in the tariff. Later on in the editorial, there is this statement:
The question is, do we Canadians really want Canada to prosper and grow? If we do, we must cut out sentiment and get down to economics. We must abandon some of our hopeless, helpless, tariff-bred weaknesses and get down to business. We have lived so long on government subvention and government protection that we have forgotten how to do business without it.
In conclusion, I believe that all members must admit the importance of motor cars and trucks in the economic and social life of this country. I think I have produced evidence to show that the prices of these articles have been advanced to the very limit allowed by the protective tariff. The ability of our
manufacturers to export their product has been amply proven, and I have also proved that the financial position of firms engaged in this industry is such that a substantial reduction in the tariff might safely be made and I believe it would be in the interest of this country if such a reduction were made.

If his statement to-night is correct it would seem that there has been some United States capital invested in the business since then. But without going into that feature, I would remind the hon. gentleman that no matter where the capital comes from, the industry gives employment to Canadian labour. There are 78 plants engaged in the manufacture of automobiles and their accessories in Canada, employing Canadian labour, and subject to Canadian taxation, a considerable amount in taxes finding sits way into the Canadian treasury.
My hon. friend quoted some prices to show the difference in value between an automobile in the United States and one of similar pattern and style in Canada. I know of course that there is some discrimination, but we account for part of it ourselves. The hon. member will bear in mind that we place a sales tax on the automobile of 5 per cent, and we also impose a luxury tax of 5 per cent on
Tariff on Automobiles

automobiles costing up to $1,200, and 10 per cent on those over $1,200. I mention this figure to remind my hon. friend that the difference in the duty, even admitting his figures does not account for the difference in the respective prices. I agree with the hon. gentleman that in many parts of Canada the automobile has become a necessity. But it is not always a necessity for there are many people owning and operating motor cars who in my opinion would be better off without them. And when I make this statement it is not because of the fact that I have never owned an automobile myself; I have never owned one for the reason that I never felt I could afford to keep and operate it. In the first place, I do not like to dig down for the price, and in the second place owning a car takes you away from your business, whether you are farmer or manufacturer, when you might well be at home. However, I will not pursue that thought further.
I wrould observe that there are two sides to the question the hon. member has advanced regarding the cost of automobiles to the Canadian people. I will admit that automobiles do cost the individual a lot of money. But I suppose that every hon. member in this House can recall the day when there were no automobiles in Canada; and when these machines were first introduced they stalled on the road about as often as they were made to go. In those early days a man who wanted an impressive turnout did not send to England for a Rolls Royce nor to the United States for a Marmon; and of course he would not have to pay any revenue to the country. What he did was to buy a pair of high steppers, so that neither the municipality nor the province got anything out of him in the way of taxes for driving his equipage along the highway. But the advent of the automobile has changed all that, and I submit that the provinces through their legislation have recognized that the automobile is a luxury, or at any rate if mot a luxury a great expense to the country.
As my hon. friend has truly said, we have in Canada a considerable number of cars. I do not remember the figures he gave but the record I have is 513,821. From the owners of these cars the provinces collect in taxes the sum of $9,290,900.82; in the Yukon Territory-and one must wonder what they can do with cars away up there-there are 86 automobiles. If we are to meet our national obligations-the interest on the national debt, the pensions that we owe to our soldiers and the widows and orphans of those who will never come back, and the cost of administration, we must have revenue from some source, and if you take away the revenue we are getting from automobiles we must secure it by imposing duties upon some other commodity. My hon. friend has suggested that we impose an additional excise tax. Well, that is a subject worth considering. We are now imposing a 5 per cent sales tax and a 5 per cent luxury tax upon automobiles up to a value of $1,200, and a further 5 per cent luxury tax upon automobiles above that value. The minister who answers for the government is content to plead the necessities of the revenue. This is the old story from protectionist Liberal governments-they cannot reduce because of the necessities of revenue. Now this government knows that there is many a schedule in the tariff to-day where reduction would add to the revenue, many a one. and I am not sure that this is not one. I do not say I am convinced it is one; but I am not sure it is not. The minister certainly did not show that it was not. The minister knows just as well as he knows he is sitting in his seat, that even though reduction may add to the revenue, it may be the worst thing in the world for the country; and that is what he should have argued before the House. That is the reason he maintains the tax where it is, and the only reason he can justify maintaining it where it is, because to do otherwise would do injury to the business of Canada. Hon. gentlemen take a single industry; they assume that the whole duty is added to the sale price, and that every manufacturer puts in his pocket that extra duty. Then they say: We paid into the manufacturer's pocket so much; we would have been better off to have paid that to the workmen and kept them in their homes idle. This simply shows an inappreciation of the whole situation. One industry depends on another; one industry makes work for another, and the loss of one industry is not the loss of one alone; it is the loss of several. The. whole thing reduces the commercial life and industrial life of the country. The minister himself takes care that he reduces no duty beyond the point that will give the industry a chance for its life, and a chance to progress and develop in this Dominion, and I would have welcomed from the minister a defence along the line that he knows to be sound-and not this lame defence behind the shade of the revenue, which he always fears is going to diminish.
Now what has been the case made out by the hon. member for Macleod? He first of all started with a quotation from this speech I made in 1911, which, if it did no other good, has constituted the intellectual nourishment of hon. gentlemen to my left for several years, a speech in which among other arguments I sought to advance for a reduction of the duty on farm implements was this one: that the hold the Canadian manufacturer 
had obtained not only on his home market but on the foreign market was such as to demonstrate that the tariff at that time was beyond the necessities of that manufacturer. I did state, and stated very plainly that he was entitled, or rather the country was entitled, to such a tariff level on the goods produced by the manufacturer of agricultural implements as would maintain his hold on the Canadian market and enable him still to advance in the markets of other countries in the world; but he was not entitled to any more. But I did not rest with that argument. I went further and produced evidence to show that factory heads in this country
10 p.m. had admitted that such had been their success under a comparatively fair tariff in developing the industry here that they were able to produce on a scale comparable with the scale in the United States, and at very little, if any, greater cost. I thought I made a pretty strong case, and I did advance facts in addition to those advanced by the hon. member for Macleod to-day. But as I said last session, and have said frequently in this House, there was, I think, one defect in the presentation I made at that time. I do not think I took into account as of sufficient strength the advantage that export trade gives the Canadian manufacturer in enabling him to increase the scale of his production, and thereby enabling him to diminish the price at home. That is the feature that everyone who is acquainted with and follows Canadian industry or that of any other country for any length of time must be impressed by, and in countries where the protection is the highest, in, for example, France to-day. In countries where the tariff wall around this country would be scarcely visible compared with theire, you do not find the people arguing that they are paying the cost of keeping up great, rich millionaire manufacturers. As a matter of fact, just because of that tariff, they to-day are able to sell and are selling within the borders of France their products at prices lower than are enjoyed by the consumers of other countries of the world, even lower than the prices that are enjoyed by Great Britain at this very time.
Now I am not certain-I certainly am not convinced by anything advanced by the Acting Minister of Finance-that it would not be possible to lower the tariff on automobiles and at the same time maintain the industry. The prices to the people in this country after the taxes are paid are in nearly every case over fifty per cent higher than in the United States. I may also say, Mr. Speaker, that the tariff on cars entering the United States is, I am told, twenty-five per cent, and it is rather strange, if a high tariff really creates low prices that we, with a tariff ten per cent higher than the United

Tariff on Automobiles

States, should pay at the factory thirty-seven per cent more for our cars than they do in the United States. I cannot understand that. The right hon. leader of the opposition said that prices were lower in France than almost any other country. Possibly that is correct, but if they are it is owing to the fact that France is working on a depreciated currency, the thing that the manufacturers and big business men and bankers in this country are so desperately afraid of, but at enables France to manufacture cheaply.
I do not wish to take time to refer to all the arguments advanced by the right hon. leader of the opposition or by the Acting Minister of Finance, but there are a few I think I should refer to very briefly. I think the first argument was that there were discrepancies in the figures which I quoted in regard to the percentage of capital in this industry which was owned in the United States: that last year I quoted it at 77.8 per cent and this year at 80 per cent. I will admit there is a discrepancy there of 2.3 per cent. I did not have the actual figures in regard to this matter. I may say it is a matter that has not been very definitely settled, but I was told a short time ago by a gentleman who has given a little study to this question that he thought it was about 80 per cent, that the establishment of American branch factories in Canada was going on all the time, and that most of the companies that were establishing branch factories over here now owned practically all the stock in their Canadian branches, but at any rate I do not think the discrepancy is big enough to make very much difference to that argument.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer very briefly to the question of motor trucks, which I think possibly I did not deal with at any great length before. I think this is a very important matter not only to farmers but to our manufacturers. They are nearly all employing motor trucks, and you can see at the present time that this duty of thirty-five per cent on motor trucks, which really amounts to thirty-seven per cent, is placing those who must buy motor trucks under a handicap, is imposing a great hardship and is very unfair to the farmers who are a long distance from railroads, and who need those motor trucks badly. I have no particuliar wish to see the duty on the high priced cars reduced. I do not think that matters very much, but I think it must be reduced on the cheaper cars. The people are demanding it, and I believe they will adopt some method of achieving that result before very long. The

Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) I think made the statement that he never owned an auto,-that he could not afford one. I would suggest that if he would reduce the duty on automobiles, he might tfe able to purchase one himself.

speechtext: I have no time to drive one.

maintopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF ON AUTOMOBILES AND MOTOR TRUCKS
speechtext:
If the Acting Minister of Finance, with a salary of $14,000 per year, feels he cannot afford a car, I would like him to consider the position of the poor farmer living fifteen or twenty miles from town. How is he going to get a car? While I am on that subject I want to refer to a very good settler in my district, a splendid type of settler, who came from Sweden-who said to me a year ago, "When I cannot afford an auto, I am going to leave the farm. I do not think I and my family should be away out here on this farm without an automobile, and I am going to leave it if I cannot make enough to keep a car." It would be good business for those people who are trying to get settlers on the land to do what I suggest if they really want them to stay on the land. The Acting Minister of Finance referred to the large tax the provinces collected out of these cars. That is only an added argument in favour of the motion which I have presented. Is the automobile to be singled out as paying the greatest tax of any industry in this country? I do not see why it should. He stated that there was a time when there were no automobiles at all. I thought he was inferring that probably those who have not automobiles ought to do without them. There was a time in this country when we did not have any railroads. Does the minister suggest that we should do all our transportation with horses again? There was a time when the farmer had no binder, no mower. Does the minister suggest that we should go back to the cradle and scythe again? He referred to the large amount of taxes which manufacturers of automobiles pay. I find in Hansard of last year, March 17, at page 379, these remarks by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), who mentions the amount of taxes some of these men pay:
During the years 1915 to 1918 inclusive a certain factory in this country produced 113,542 automobiles, and the excess price charged to Canadian purchasers over the prevailing price in the United States was $13,394,941. The wages paid by that concern during that period on the cars actually made and sold in Canada amounted to $9,083,360, and their total wage $11,960,807. That is their total wage bill on cars made for sale in Canada and for export. They paid in taxes during that period $2,285,145, leaving a surplus of $2,027,436. What do these figures mean? They mean that during this period the people of Canada would have paid all the wages this firm

Tariff on Automobiles
paid, all the 1axes this firm paid, and had a surplus in the national treasury of $2,027,436, or a sum sufficient in itself to pay more than half the duty paid by this firm on their raw material entering into the manufacture of this article.
I regret that the Acting Minister of Finance did not give a 'little more consideration to my proposal for increasing the excise tax so as to make up any loss of revenue that would occur through the reduction in the tariff. He simply said that it was worth considering, and I suppose he thinks we should be satisfied with that. I hope he will consider it.
I am disappointed at the attitude taken by the Acting Minister of Finance, and if this government will not reduce the duty on automobiles and trucks, particularly trucks and lower priced cars, it should give up all pretence of making any reduction in the tariff. As regards the actual reduction, the motion, as worded, leaves it to the interpretation of the government, if the resolution should be fortunate enough to be passed by this House. I do not think it would be my place to say what amount should be taken off the present duty, but something very substantial should be taken off in regard to lower priced cars and trucks. Personally, I do not care whether anything is taken off the higher priced cars or not. When I come to eastern Canada and visit the cities, Ottawa included, I am always struck by the large number of handsome, high priced cars that are driven around the streets. The government would save some money on their own high priced cars if they would reduce the duty. When I see the number of old, dilapidated, practically worn-out cars that are in use in some of the rural sections of Canada, I cannot help feeling that there is something very wrong in this country. People out in the country doing at least their fair share of the work are not getting a fair return. It may be hard to convince hon. members who spend most of the time in these cities that there is any necessity for reducing these duties, but if they will visit the rural sections and see the cars that some people are using and the number of people who are not able to purchase cars at all, they would be ready to give t'heir approval to this resolution.
As a final word, I would say that I hope the majority of the members to-night will give their support to this resolution, because it is something that the people of Canada generally would appreciate and they would back up those members who would support such a resolution.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (North Toronto) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for Canada to have a national policy in rela-

tion to its coal supply and that no part of Canada should be left dependent upon the United States for such supply.
The government should immediately consider the initiation of an all British and Canadian coal supply and that such a policy is both a social and economic necessity and in the best interests of the future of Canada.
That a duty should be placed on coal from the United States to ensure an all British supply for Canada and thus afford adequate protection to coal mined and coked under the British flag.
That, whereas coal is in effect a food, it should be carried on a preferential toll basis by the railways on the same basis as food.
He said: I do not propose to make any lengthy speech to-night on this subject inasmuch as my views are already recorded in Hansard. For three sessions now I have brought this matter to t'he attention of parliament and I have already given at some length my reasons for the proposal I make in this resolution. Since last session some $200,000 has been voted as a bonus for the carrying of coal from Alberta and the Maritime provinces to central Canada, but we have not had any particulars as to how that money was spent. I understand that it was devoted altogether to the carrying of coal from the Mari times to the province of Quebec. The resolution, as will be observed, also relates to an embargo on coal. It is my opinion that a duty should be imposed on coal coming from the United States in order to ensure an all British supply for Canada. We want to develop our own resources, and I think it is necessary that we should have some adequate protection so that all the coal Canada uses will be mined and coked under the British flag. Recently some supporters of the government in the Maritime provinces, notably Premier Armstrong, have been inviting the government to impose a duty on coal in order to stimulate the industry in that part of the country. Some five million tons of coal are used in the province of Quebec annually and of this only two millions come from1 the Maritime provinces, the other three millions from the United States. As I said a moment ago, I do not intend1 to discuss the subject of this resolution at any length seeing that the principle of it was adopted last session by a unanimous vote of the House, that is to say, as regards the desirability of having a national policy in relation to the mining of coal in Canada. The reasons I gave for a national coal policy for Canada are the same to-night as those that I have advanced during the past three years in parliament, and are so well understood by the House, that I will not labour the matter further. I will simply content myself tonight with moving the resolution for a na-

National Coal Policy
tional policy for Canada so that every ton of coal used in Canada shall be mined and coked under the British flag whether it is from Wales, Alberta or the Maritime provinces thus keeping labour and wages in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The resolution
which the 'hon. gentleman has moved, except in regard to the question of the imposition of the duty, was adopted by the House last session, and with that single exception the government will offer no objection to the motion. The question of an increase of duty is however a departure from the principle that was voted upon last session, and I may say frankly that the government do not feel that they can agree to the levying of a greater duty. It is quite true that Premier Armstrong and a number of the coal operators and other interested parties came from Nova Scotia to interview the government during the recess. They asked for an increase in t'he duty on slack coal from fourteen to fifty-three cents, and that is the only request they made with respect to the imposition of a duty.
It strikes me as being too late in the evening to discuss this coal proposition thoroughly. It is a matter that I have given a great deal of attention to during the past two years. Last session the House voted a subvention of $200,000 to assist in the transportation of coal. Owing to the strike in Alberta last year no arrangement was made for the transportation of coal during t'he season when it could be economically hauled 'by the railways. Later in the year when in western Canada I had an interview with Premier Greenfield at which Sir Henry Thornton and Mr. Stutchbury, the fuel commissioner for Alberta, were present. It was then decided that although the mines were again under way and producing coal, it was getting too close to the season when the wheat movement would begin for the railways to embark on the experiment to establish the freight rate on coal from Alberta to Ontario. Alberta coal has been used in all parts of Ontario to the entire satisfaction of everyone. The question is one of freight rates and freight rates alone. Let me say for the information of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) and other hon. members that we have agreed to have the experiment carried on this spring. I suggested there should be an arrangement that the coal should be mined and placed on board car at $3.50 a ton, that the railways should be handed the coal in trainload lots to be carried to common distributing points in Ontario, and that every
facility should be given to try to establish a lower rate than that prevailing. Sir Henry Thornton intimated at the interview that the lowest rate at which the railways could transport that coal was $9 a ton. I see by press despatches that catne through no later than yesterday-I have not received the information in any other way-that negotiations between the Alberta government and the railway are proceeding and that they propose establishing a rate of $7 a ton for the trial shipment of 50,000' tons. That shipment, as I say will be made next, spring. It is estimated that if a rate of $6 a ton could be granted, and if the mining and loading on car could be done at $3.50 per ton, it would make it possible to bring Alberta coal into Ontario and meet the competition of American anthracite.
In the investigations carried on by the Dominion Fuel Board we have been devoting our attention to see if it is not possible to supplant anthracite coal coming from the United States into the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Naturally fuel coming from Alberta will be largely, if not altogether, lignite suitable for domestic purposes, and we hope it will supplant, the American anthracite supplied to those provinces.
The coal fields of Nova Scotia have been having rather a difficult time. This year we offered them a subvention to assist them in getting their coal to points further west to the extent of 50 cents a ton as the maximum on any shipment. I am sorry I did not know this resolution was coming up to-night or I would have had full details for my hon. friend; I will be prepared to lay them on the table of the House before very many days showing exactly what has happened. Briefly, Mr. Speaker, it is estimated that we have extended the market for Nova Scotia coal 100 miles westward by the assistance given to the coal movement.
To what points?

speechtext: As far west as Cornwall, and in a line directly north of Cornwall.

Mr. STEW'ART (Argenteuil):	When investigation was made the price of coal in Montreal and Toronto was about $6 a ton; they were both about on a parity. But that only comes about owing to the facilities provided for water shipment. With reference to the question by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), we do hope to supplant all the anthracite coal coming from the United States by providing a cheaper product. That is another experiment we have been carrying on. I may say that I hope to continue the subvention to assist in the transportation of coal this year, and I also hope to bring down legislation for the assistance of the manufacture of coke, to which we have been devoting a very great deal of attention recently. My hon. friend is probably aware that in the city of Hamilton there is a splendid by-product coal manufacturing plant that is giving excellent service and producing a fuel from bituminous and low grade coals which is superior to the anthracite and which can be produced at from $2.50 to $3 per ton less. So 
we hope to convert a product that is plentiful, in which there is not liable to be a famine. The anthracite field of the United States is becoming somewhat depleted and in all probability in the very near future we will be faced by an embargo on their anthracite coming into Canada. So we have been working along the line of the conversion of bituminous fuel into high grade coke for domestic purposes. There is always some difficulty; these small tests are not always successful from the commercial point of view. But the transference of bituminous coal into coke is no longer an experiment; its success has been amply demonstrated and the resulting fuel has proved its superiority over anthracite. WTe know now that this is the solution of the problem of supplanting the present anthracite fuel supply throughout Ontario and Quebec,
The coking will have to be done here in the central provinces?

speechtext:
Yes. If
we can transfer Nova Scotia fuel into high grade coke say in Quebec-at Montreal, perhaps, where there is a market for the byproducts-we can use a million and a half tons of that coal to take the place of anthracite coal at present coming from the south to this part of the country. That is what we hope to do. I intend to bring down legislation at a later day, of which I will give due notice, and we can then discuss the matter more fully.

The amount of coke that
could be profitably produced would necessarily depend upon the extent of the market for the by-products?

Perhaps my hon. friend is aware that at present the Ontario Hj'dro-Eleetric people are seriously considering the establishment of a large steam plant to supplement their hydro operation in Toronto and vicinity. The larger cities throughout the eastern provinces-Ottawa, Montreal, Quebec and so on-would eonswme all the by-products resulting from the coking of a million and a half

tons of Nova Scotia coal which now has difficulty in finding a market, and we would then be put beyond the necessity of looking to the American market for anthracite fuel. So much for the eastern area; and if we can make a success of the transporting of Alberta coal into the northern and western portions of Ontario, then we can cover the whole field so far as domestic fuel is concerned.

minister's remarks regarding Alberta coal, did I understand him to say that 50,000 tons of coal were to be shipped?

have pointed out, the whole matter was held up in Alberta last summer when the shipment could have been undertaken, owing to the strike. When the strike was over it was thought to be too late in the

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
speechtext:
I was not aware, Mr. Speaker, that the resolution standing in the
name of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) would be taken up this evening, and I am not prepared to discuss the question in detail as I should like to do. There are, however, a few observations which I desire to make with respect to the resolution so far as it pertains to the question of duty on coal. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), I think it was, during the course of a discussion in the House on another subject, asked me where I stood on the question of coal duties. I am always prepared, Mr. Speaker, to say where I stand on any queition when the proper time comes, and to-night I am going to express my views, for what they are worth, with regard to the question of duty as it affects slack coal in the province of Nova Scotia. I shall also have something to say as regards the duty on coal as it would affect the western provinces if the duty on slack coal was made as I think it should be.
Let me outline briefly the history of the duty on coal. In 1879 a duty of 50 cents a ton was imposed on all coal imported into this country, whether anthracite, bituminous or coal dust. A year or so later, about 1880, this duty was increased to 60 cents a ton on all kinds of coal imported. In 1894 further changes were made in the tariff: the duty on bituminous coal was left at 60 cents a ton; the duty on coal dust-which meant, I presume, what we now call slack coal-was placed at 20 per cent ad valorem, and anthracite was put on the free list. There was, of course, a reason why anthracite was put on the free list. We do not mine anthracite coal in Canada. So far as our geologists have been able to establish up to the present time we have not anywhere in Canada anthracite coal of the quality of that which we import from the United States. It therefore became a dire necessity in Ontario and the western parts of Quebec-in fact, everywhere in Canada, but particularly those sections-to get the best fuel at the lowest possible rate, and I presume that is why in 1894, the government of the day saw fit to remove the duty on anthracite coal. The duty has remained off anthracite coal from that time to this.
In 1906 there was another change in the duty on coal. Slack coal was given a duty of 14 cents a ton. This was coal that would go through a screen with a half inch mesh-the requirement had previously been three-quarters of an inch, I believe. Run of mine and screened bituminous coal was loft at 53 cents a ton. In those days slack coal was scarcely marketable in this country, and I am going to point out an anomaly that grew up. Slack
National Coal Policy

coal in those days carried an ad valorem duty of 20 per cent and the slack coal that came in here was so cheap that the government of the day finally set a recognized value of 65 cents a ton on all slack coal imported. So it was a very cheap commodity in those days, because it was not used for any particular purpose. That ad valorem duty of 20 per cent on 65 cents made the duty 13 cents per ton, and in 1906-1907 the duty was made 14 cents a ton. I want to point out that the duty on run of mine coal or screened bituminous coal, and the duty on slack coal, presents to-day an anomalous situation which cannot be understood in this country. Slack coal to-day is practically as valuable as run of mine coal, for the reason that the manufacturers in central Canada have so developed their plants that they can use slack coal better than run of mine or screened bituminous coal. As a matter of fact, many of them break up their run of mine or screened coal into very fine dust, which they use in their furnaces.
Another point is this: It is said on the very best authority that large coal barges come from the United States across the Great Lakes to Montreal, and these boats are divided into two compartments. One compartment contains say 2,000 tons of slack coal, which comes into this country at a duty of 14 cents a ton, and the other compartment contains run of mine or screened bituminous coal, which carries a duty of 53 cents a ton. That coal is taken to the dock at Montreal-and I am speaking of Montreal because it is the largest consumer of this sort of coal-and the duty is paid, and then the slack coal and the screened coal is mixed and sold in Montreal as run of mine coal. It could not all come in as run of mine coal or it would have to pay a duty of 53 cents a ton; but by mixing it they pay only 14 cents on half the cargo and 53 cents on the other half, and then the whole cargo is mixed and sold as run of mine coal in Montreal. I say that is a fraud on the customs of this country; but it is being done. The only way to stop it is to level up the duty on slack coal from 14 cents to 53 cents. I am not going into a lengthy argument, but I stand for that because I think it is fair, and because I think it will bring the duty on coal up to a point where we will be able to get a bigger market in Montreal for our slack coal. Slack coal constitutes, I am told in some cases as high as 55 per cent of the output of certain of our mines in Nova Scotia; in many of the mines with which I am more familiar I know it constitutes at least 40 per cent of their output.

I agree with those who say that we should give to the people of this country fuel at the very lowest possible cost.. I agree with those who say we should not raise the duty on coal to such a point that the people in central Canada might be, so to speak, crucified in the matter of heating their homes, or the manufacturers of this country, who are entitled to a fair deal, charged too much. But I say that if the government imposed this duty they would be doing nobody any harm. The bogey of British Columbia and of Alberta is set up, and I will tell you why. In British Columbia they have a market for considerable of their slack coal in the United States. Their coal goes into the United States at 14 cents a ton for slack coal, and run of mine at 53 cents a ton, exactly the same duty as coal carries entering this countiy. Now if we raise the duty on slack coal to 53 cents, which is where the duty on bituminous coal stands to-day, the American duty would go up to the same point, and our British Columbia friends argue that their export trade to the United States would be injured. But may I point out that British Columbia is in an entirely different position in this respect from Nova Scotia, and also Alberta. If you will look at the map, you will see that Washington and Idaho are the states adjoining British Columbia, and in neither Washington nor Idaho is there any quantity of slack coal, scarcely any in fact; and if the Americans over there are taking slack coal to-day from British Columbia, a duty of 53 cents a ton would not prevent British Columbia coal from entering those two states, because from its geographical position British Columbia would continue to enjoy the identical market it has to-day.

Are there any
large importations of coal there?
There is very little slack coal imported, but they use some in their factories.

Is it not true that if Canada imposes a tariff duty on slack coal, then under the reciprocal agreement the United States will impose a corresponding duty on our coal entering that country, and would not that react against our coal entering the Washington market?

I said that was the argument, but perhaps not as well as my hon. friend has said it. I said that the moment we place a duty of 53 cents a ton on slack coal entering this country, a similar duty will be placed on our exportations of Slack coal to the United States; but I also said that from

National Coal Policy
the geographical position of British Columbia in relation to the states of Washington and Idaho, British Columbia is not going to lose any market they have to-day for their coal by reason of that additional duty being levied. Alberta is in perhaps a little different position.
I do not know what percentage of the coal of Alberta is slack coal, but I do know that some of the states adjoining Alberta are in the very same geographical position relative to Alberta as are Washington and Idaho with relation to British Columbia, and if we should Level up the duty on slack coal entering this country to where it should be, and where it was at one time, and do away with this anomalous situation that exists to-day, I do not think it would hinder one ton of Alberta coal going to the states adjoining.
A year or two ago, in 1923 I think it was, representatives of the miners of Alberta came to this government and took up the question of lignite. I am not speaking by the book, but I think Alberta is the only province that has any amount of lignite coal, and they have a chance of getting a market for that in the United States. We do not import any lignite from the United States that I know of; if we import any, it is only a very small quantity. Those of us interested in coal made no kick when Alberta asked for the removal of the duty on lignite, in order that the reciprocal agreement which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) has mentioned might apply and the lignite of Alberta enter the United States free, it is done to-day, and as far as lignite is concerned, I believe it did the industry of Alberta some considerable good.
Speaking about Alberta, I said a moment ago that I was sorry my hon. friend brought up this resolution so late at night. I sent up for my papers but have not got them yet. I have a copy of a resolution passed by the Edmonton Board of Trade in December to the effect that they stood for the levelling u,p of the duty on slack coal to where the duty on ordinary run of mine and screened bituminous coal stood. I observe one of two of my hon. friends from the west smilling. I do not know the complexion of the Edmonton Board of Trade, but it seems to me that the boards of trade in the west probably are composed of business men, as boards of trade in central and eastern Canada are, and I would think that before the Edmonton Board of Trade would seriously propose and pass a resolution of this kind, they would consider what the effect of it would be on the slack coal industry of Alberta. I am taking for granted that, having passed that resolution, agreeing that it was an anomalous position for
this country to occupy in regard to its coal trade, that they must have given very serious consideration to the question of how the levelling up of the duty on slack coal would affect the slack coal industry in Alberta; and I am concluding that, after having given it that consideration, they must have come to the conclusion that it would not affect that industry to the disadvantage of the miners or operators of the province of Alberta.
I say that it is an anomalous position for the government of this country to occupy. It is going to help our coal industry in Nova Scotia and it is not going to affect disastrously the coal industry in either British Columbia or in Alberta, which are the other two great sources of supply. I point out this fact, tha* in the past year we did not come within
1,350,000	tons of the quantity of coal used on the Montreal market, as compared with the quantity used in 1923. We were about 1,400,000 tons short on the Montreal market, and I believe had we mined that 1,400.000 tons and placed it on the Montreal market, there would not be the distress which exists in certain areas of Nova Scotia and especially in Cape Breton. It is reckoned by those who are in the trade that they could market one million tons of slack coal in the district of Montreal. They could land it there for distribution if the duty on slack coal were levelled up to where it should be. I could give the House innumerable figures in this regard. I am simply placing myself where I think every Nova Scotian should be placed, I say that they should stand for the levelling up of the duty on slack coal from fourteen to fift3^-three cents per ton.
What about reducing the other?

If we are going to have
any duties in this country I believe in having them uniform. We buy practically every suit of clothes, almost all our shoes, all our manufactured goods in Canada from manufacturers who are protected in the market to the extent of twenty-five to thirty-five per cent ad valorem duty, and we in Nova Scotia who have to buy those goods bearing that duty are in the position of getting between a five and ten per cent ad valorem duty on coal. If my hon. friend wishes to suggest that we in Nova Scotia should occupy that position relatively to the people of the central provinces, then I say to him that he is not a good Maritime man. The farmers of the country have thirty per cent on their goods. My western friends say they do not want it. I say nothing about that. They know more about it than I do.
National Coal Policy

I am talking of a matter which I know something about.
With reference to the subvention granted last year in the matter of rates on coal to points west of Riviere du Loup, I want to point out what a very small thing is capable of accomplishing. This subvention was voted about the 15th or 16th of July, and did not become effective till the latter part of July. This government voted $200,000 and gave a subvention of one fifth of one cent per ton per mile for every ton of coal which came west of Riviere d'u Loup. What was the result of that? It was a very small thing, but ,it enabled the coal operators of Nova Scotia to market in that short period, from the latter part of July to the close of navigation, one hundred thousand tons of coal in the market west of Montreal which market up to that time they were never able to reach. That was what the subvention meant to us. We are thankful to the government for what they did last year. It will mean a great deal more this year because the operators can take advantage of that one-fifth of one cent per mile from the very opening of navigation to the close, and if we go by comparisons, it would not surprise ime if this enabled them to reach, perhaps, with two hundred thousand tons of coal this year, markets which they were unable to reach some years ago.
I am in perfect harmony also with the project to establish coking plants. I am proud of the fact that I raised this very question in the House in the session of 1922. I gave it as my opinion then that the only way to combat in this country the high price of anthracite coal was for this government, or any other government that might be in power, to have some great national policy on the question of coking; so that the people of Ontario and Quebec and the other provinces that are forced to use anthracite coal might be given something as good as anthracite at two or three dollars a ton cheaper. I was glad to hear the Minister of Mines (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) say to-night that that was the policy of the government, and I am proud to be in a position to say that it was I who brought this to the attention of the government in the session of 1922. I believe it will work marvels in connection with the coal trade, in giving the people of this country a cheaper fuel as good as anthracite. It will work marvels in doing the very thing which my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) had in view every time he moved this resolution in the last two or three years for a national policy on the question of a supply of coal for Canada. The trouble with

the proposition, Mr. Speaker, is that, as with all other innovations, it will probably take some considerable time to work out, and to get men sufficiently interested to place their money in it. But I am given to understand by some financial men who to-day have nothing to do with coal operations that, if a proper bill is brought down this session in connection with coking plants, it will work marvels in giving the miners of Nova Scotia and, I am in hopes, the miners of Alberta, when they have proper freight rates, a chance of getting clear of their surplus of slack coal which, at the present time, they are unable to market in the large centres of Canada. This may take two or three years, and in the meantime we are at the mercy of United States operators.
While I am a low tariff man, while I voted to-night for the reduction especially on trucks, as I did not swallow the whole of my hon. friend's resolution and while I believe motor trucks which come into this country for business purposes should come in at a reduced rate of duty in order that business men, farmers and others who require trucks in their actual business may get them a little cheaper, I do not think this is the time that we should have lower tariffs in view of what our neighbours to the south have been doing with their tariff for the last two or three years. In Nova Scotia we are practically shut out from the markets which we had there for our fresh fish. The result to-day is that men who were engaged in the fishing trade along the south coast of Nova Scotia and particularly the island of Cape Breton, are forced out of that business for want of a market and they must go to the coal mines of Nova Scotia to make a living, as that is the only other large industry we have. If I had time I might go into the way in which our customs officials are looking after the dumping clause of the act. We are not well organized in this regard, and I am of opinion to-day that this is one of the things that should be remedied owing to the fact that while United States' operators are not dumping their coal into this country, they are defrauding the tariff getting it in at a much lower duty than it should come in at. I hope I have satisfied the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), who asked me the other night regarding my position in regard to the question of coal duty. I have placed it before the House in a much briefer way than I would like to have done, owing to the fact, as I said at the outset, that I was unaware that this question was coming before the House this evening.

Mr. Speaker, I was wondering if the Minister

National Coal Policy
of the Interior could clear up a little confusion that seems to exist between this government and the provincial government. I understand when he was out west recently he made a speech in which he made nearly the same statement as he has made to-night. I have before me a copy of the Edmonton Journal in which there is a report of an interview with Premier Greenfield of Alberta, who states that they knew nothing about any $50,000 being specially ear-marked for moving Alberta coal.
I do not wish to read these articles as they are a little long, but further down, on April 28, the trade commissioner, Mr. Stutchlbury, says that he wrote the Hon. Mr. Stewart asking for this assistance, and that on June 23 he renewed the request, so I cannot see how the minister can state to-night that he did not have any application from Alberta.
