Mr. Speaker, when the subvention was voted last year, both the Alberta government and the eastern coal interests knew it was for the purpose of assisting in transportation. When we passed the order in council after a definite arrangement had been made for the assistance of eastern coal, we set aside $50,000 to be applied to the movement from Alberta.
It was always there. The one difficulty was that arrangements were made to call on the government to put up the amount. Furthermore, I told Mr. Stutdhbury, the trade commissioner, last spring, while the strike was on, that I would expect lignite coal would be loaded at a rate of $3.50 per ton. He doubted very much whether that could be secured. Mr. Speaker, the issue is extremely plain, and it affords us a pretty good opportunity of showing whether there is any real sympathy in this House with Nova Scotia and Nova Scotia miners, some of that sympathy that we have heard so much about from people that I had hopes (were entirely sincere
in their expressions of sympathy. The minister gives us very cheering news in connection with coking. It is a very excellent thing, something which we certainly ought to have. The minister said that there was another good thing about coking besides supplying this coke. He said it would also enable the Nova Scotia people, who now have considerable difficulty in finding a market, to sell another million and a 'half tons of coal. The hon. gentleman nods his head. When the hon. gentleman said that, he admitted the necessity for the duty. When he nods his head, he corroborates the necessity for the duty-

speechtext: No.

-and yet he tells us that there should be no duty. He shook his head. Let us see why he did so. In the first instance, as we understand the matte!, there is difficulty in Canadians selling bituminous coal in this country, while at the same time we are importing millions and millions of tons of bituminous coal. Under those circumstances, if anything like a fair consideration be given, if the question of Canadian markets for the Canadian worker is to apply at all, surely it is supposed to be the policy of this government that it should apply in matters that are indigenous, in matters of first production, the mines, agriculture, fisheries and forests. Certainly we have in the mines in Nova Scotia a condition which is such that the companies cannot market their coal, and my hon. friend knows that. He knows further that not only can the companies not market their coal, but .that they have banked coal and this means loss in the coal itself, deterioration of the coal, losses in the trade. My hon. friend has also admitted that it costs $6 a ton to put Nova Scotia coal into Montreal. If he has looked into the matter at all he will know, what is the fact, that American bituminous can be sold easily at lower rates, and that company contracts are given freely on that reduced Scale. I do not really know why the government wants the reference to the duty withdrawn; I cannot see the reason. Here we have something which is absolutely indigenous to the soil, something which is intensely vital to a whole province; we have something passed upon by the Liberal party of that province through its official chief in regard to which there is a demand for a duty. We are not asking for any specific duty in this matter. We are merely asking that there be a protective duty which will enable Canadians to work in Canada. It does seem to me that under these circumstances the gov-
National Coal Policy

eminent, if they desire to give any consideration at all to the Nova Scotia miners, will accept the resolution.

I want
to have a little information regarding this resolution; I want to know exactly what a national policy in regard to fuel means. The resolution calls for a duty on United States coal; but that cannot possibly help the householder, whether in Ontario or in western Canada. In this country we are in the anomalous position of having created an industrial area that possesses neither coal nor steel, an industrial area that is devoid of these two great commodities necessary to a manufacturing centre. The situation regarding fuel is acute only in this area of Ontario. Now, if a national policy on fuel means that the treasury must again be drained in order to give a subsidy to the railways to haul coal from Alberta and from Nova Scotia, I think we should carefully consider it before entering on this kind of project. This industrial area, as I have said, is in a most anomalous position. The fuel situation no doubt is sometimes acute, but we cannot better it by this means; and after we have protected this area by a high tariff from competition without, and also by means of a discriminatory freight rate from competition on the part of the rest of the Dominion, I for one will want to know exactly what a national policy on fuel means. I see it calls for a duty, and it also calls for a preferential rate on the railways. Western Canada will not be in favour of this resolution, and I for one must oppose it.
Mr. HANCE J. LOGAN (Cumberland): It is now nearly midnight, and this is no time to discuss a national coal policy. I regret that we have not a whole day to consider the matter in view of its supreme importance. I shall not take more than a few minutes therefore to express my opinion on the subject. Last year when the resolution was moved, I endeavoured, speaking at some length, to show the necessity for a readjustment of the coal tariff.
We are asking in Nova Scotia that the duty on Slack coal be made the same as that on run of mine. When run of mine coal was given a duty of fifty-three cents a ton, a duty was placed on slack coal of fourteen cents, the idea being that the tariff from an ad valorem standpoint was about equal; because at that time slack coal was a cheap commodity. As a matter of fact, if you travelled throughout the United States then you would find around every colliery mountains of slack coal which you could buy at fifty cents or 
less a ton. Owing to improved apparatus, however, stokers, feeders and so on, slack coal has become almost as valuable as run of mine, so that to-day there is only a few cents difference in the price. And yet the duty on slack coal remains at only fourteen cents a ton as against fifty-three cents on run of mine. We in Nova Scotia are asking that the relative' ad valorem percentage be made the same as it was when the duty was established. I do not think we are asking anything unreasonable; I do not think that an increase in duty will affect the consumers of this country to any great extent. But we shall certainly prevent the fraud on customs referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll), whereby importers to-day make a mixture of about half slack and half run of mine. They screen it at the mine in Pennsylvania and enter it for customs about half slack and half run of mine. The actual duty they pay is about thirty-three cents a ton. Thirty-three cents a ton on coal at the price it is to-day is not a protective tariff.
Let me read, for the information of the House, some figures in regard to the value per ton compared to the percentage of duty as collected on run of mine coal and slack coal. In 1916 the percentage of duty to value was 46.5 per cent, on run of mine. In
1923	it had gone down to 13.5 per cent. In
1924	the percentage of duty collected on the value of run of mine was 17.7. In 1916 the percentage of duty to value on slack coal was 162 per cent; in 1923 it was 3.8 per cent, and in 1924 5.9 per cent. In that time the importation of slack coal had increased by leaps and bounds until last year there was imported into this country over 3,000,000 tons of slack bituminous coal, paying a duty of only 5.9 per cent of the value. Yet when we in Nova Scotia ask for an increase in that duty we are charged with being high protectionists. We are only asking for the lowest kind of revenue tariff on slack coal
We know to-night something of the conditions that exist in some of the collieries of eastern Canada. I will not go over the harrowing state of affairs that prevails there, and which existed even before the strike. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that whereas Nova Scotia in 1913, the last normal year- that is, the last year before the war-produced over 8,000,000 short tons of coal, in 1924 we produced only 5,500,000 short tons. In other words, our production of coal in Nova Scotia instead of advancing, as it should have done, has gone down since 1913 two and a half million tons annually. And yet you want to know what is the reason for the conditions

National Coal Policy
that prevail in Nova Scotia to-day! One of the chief reasons why there has been that great decrease in production is the admission of slack coal at a very low rate of duty. We are now asking that that be rectified and the duty upon all coal put at the same rate.
I go further, although all my friends do not agree with me, and say that when we need a tariff so badly that we are taxing our people here, there and everywhere in all sorts of ways, we should insist on putting a duty upon what is a semi-luxury-anthracite coal. No man can advance any argument in favour of the policy that makes the poor man who lives in a hovel pay a duty upon his coal while the man who lives in a mansion is allowed to bring in his coal duty free. I also advocate of course that we should put a duty upon anthracite dust, because that is another commodity which came in here last year to the extent of 300,000 or 400,000 tons to supplant coal mined by the miners of Canada.
Now, what is the objection to this course? The only objection I have heard raised is that if we increased the duty on slack coal the Americans would also increase the duty upon slack coal from British Columbia. If I am wrong I want to be corrected, but I am informed that, whereas in Nova Scotia we produce over 40 per cent of slack coal owing to the friable condition of our coal, in British Columbia they do not produce more then 20 per cent of slack coal, nearly all of which they use for manufacturing purposes in that province. They are not sending slack coal from British Columbia into the United States. Therefore there is nothing to fear in the way of reprisals.
I congratulate the government upon the policy they propose to adopt with reference to coking. It is a policy which can be discussed at considerable length when the measure is brought down. I endorsed the policy last year of giving a subvention in aid of freight rates on coal. It has brought good results, for over 100,000 tons of coal have reached Quebec and Ontario from Nova Scotia that would never have been sent there but for that subvention. I wish, however, that the limit of 50 cents could be increased to at least SI, because under the present rate no coal has been shipped from the mainland of Nova Scotia into, these western markets. This matter will take considerable time to debate, and I am not going to weary the House at this late hour. I only make this plea to the government, to remember that we have in Nova Scotia 14,000 honest, hardworking men-that is, they would like to work if conditions were right. We have down there
men who have been mining coal under difficult circumstances, and we find that instead of our production going up it has gone down two and a half million tons per annum during the past twelve years. Taking the average price of coal at the mine at S4 per ton, we are receiving $10,000,000 less in Nova Scotia in 1925 than we were in 1913.

Mr. Speaker, this is a large question, and it has been discussed from several angles this evening. Most of those who have spoken have viewed it from the standpoint of the mine operators and the miners. Now, a large body of people are vitally interested in this question-the people who consume coal. Nearly everybody does that. This is a country in which artificial heat must be provided during the winter months, and I know as a matter of fact that the ordinary householder in the Maritime provinces finds it difficult at the present price of coal to 'warm his house sufficiently to make it comfortable. He finds his coal the largest item in his bill of expense. Therefore I should like to say something from his viewpoint. But the evening is so late, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot do the subject justice, and therefore I move the adjournment of the debate.
